records.content: The sweeter side of veterinary medicine Welcome to your new favorite place to grow in vet med. Discover brilliant experts, engaging videos, interactive quizzes, inspiring stories, and podcasts that keep you curious, connected, and excited about what's next. After serving in the U.S. Navy, raising a family while earning her veterinary degree, and drawing inspiration from her immigrant mother's entrepreneurial journey, Dr. Lieu Balu is preparing to lead her own veterinary clinic in Phoenix. Scientists detect H5 bird flu antibodies in apparently healthy Greenland polar bears, raising new concerns about wildlife disease spread in the Arctic. Ask most people what a veterinary pathologist does all day and they’ll probably picture microscopes, slides, cells, and very serious diagnostic reports. Dr. Aleksandra Zuraw certainly does all of that. New research involving nearly 900 dogs reveals that larger breeds don't just have shorter lives. Their bodies may actually age faster at the molecular level, and the discovery could change how scientists approach canine longevity. H5N1 bird flu strikes Minnesota turkey and Indiana duck farms as another Texas dairy herd tests positive, raising new concerns for veterinarians. LMU researchers challenge a decades-old model: genetically modified embryos lacking interferon tau can establish pregnancies and develop into healthy calves. A landmark Purina study found that lean Labrador Retrievers lived 1.8 years longer and developed chronic disease later. Here's why the findings still matter for veterinarians 25 years later. Scientists warn that emerging African swine fever variants could undermine vaccine protection, making surveillance and biosecurity more important than ever. Letter of Reasonable Assurance clears the way for Maryland’s first in-state veterinary school to begin recruiting and admitting its inaugural class in 2027 11 careers. 6 questions. Zero chill. Veterinary medicine isn't one job—it's about eleven careers hiding under the same white coat. There is a conversation happening in break rooms, group chats, and parking lots all over veterinary medicine. It usually starts the same way. I love the medicine, but I do not know how much longer I can do this. And it usually ends with a quiet assumption that something is wrong with the person saying it. Somewhere along the way, veterinary medicine developed an unwritten rule: clinical practice is the real job, and everything else is quitting. It gets absorbed in school, reinforced in practice, and carried around as guilt by veterinarians who are exhausted, curious, or simply ready for a change but afraid that stepping out of the exam room means abandoning their oath. If you are graduating this year, the offers are probably already arriving, and some of the numbers are eye-watering. Signing bonuses have become the headline of new grad recruitment, and with student debt where it is, nobody could blame you for reading the biggest number and reaching for a pen. Vet school can turn almost anything into a performance metric. Grades, class rank, clinical skills, productivity, sleep, exercise, and sometimes even food can quietly become one more thing you feel like you should be “doing right.” Add long days, irregular schedules, stress, limited money, constant comparison, and a culture that can reward pushing through discomfort, and it is easy for a complicated relationship with food or your body to hide in plain sight. There are queer and trans veterinarians who came before you, students at other schools experiencing many of the same things, peer-support volunteers willing to listen, community organizations that know your city, and national groups that can help when a problem becomes medical, legal, academic, or overwhelming. Vet school has a way of eating your entire calendar. Between exams, labs, rotations, boards, jobs, relationships, and trying to get enough sleep to remain functional, personal health can slide down the priority list pretty quickly. There is a particular kind of kitchen alchemy that happens when nothing gets thrown away: a roast chicken becomes dinner, then lunch, then the broth for Thursday's ramen. A single Sunday afternoon becomes a month of breakfasts. What follows is not a diet plan so much as a system, one built on a $500 monthly grocery budget, a single person's appetite, and the stubborn belief that homemade is both cheaper and better. Meet Mecca Gladney, a first-generation college graduate, mother, and University of Arizona veterinary student pursuing a career in veterinary surgery while championing representation, mentorship, and mental health. The UC Davis veterinary student took a winding road to her dream school, but every setback helped shape the veterinarian and mentor she hopes to become. Now Monika Lagarejos wants to use her place in veterinary medicine to care for animals, strengthen communities, and make sure the next generation of future veterinarians knows they belong. McPaul Hermoso started veterinary school at 35 after earning multiple degrees and living in five countries. Discover his unconventional journey, lifelong dream of becoming a veterinarian, and mission to inspire others. From four years cheering at LSU to studying veterinary medicine at the Royal Veterinary College, Jalyne Blackwell is building a career by saying yes to the opportunities that scare her a little—and trusting that the unexpected path might be the right one. After France’s competitive exams shut the door, this 20-year-old found her calling 800 miles from home — and proof that a detour can still lead exactly where you were meant to go. Meet Taja Bell, an LSU veterinary student, Army Animal Care Specialist, mom and model working toward a future in emergency medicine and surgery. There is a particular kind of courage it takes to walk away from a career you have already proven yourself in and start over as a first-year student. Emese Avdeyenkova has done exactly that, twice over, once when she traded a biology degree for an Army uniform, and again when she traded that uniform for a white coat. Now she is bringing all of it, the discipline, the humility, and the hard-won perspective, to Vet Candy Radio as one of the vet student hosts of Vet School After Dark. America's favorite vet receptionist Caitlin Palmer and her cat daddy husband Clay Palmer dig into the real science, history, and psychology behind humanity's longest-running obsession. We're talking ancient Egypt, where cats were literally worshipped as gods. We're talking the internet, where cats generate more content than almost anything else on the planet. From ancient worship to TikTok stardom, cats have clawed their way into our hearts and honestly, they never asked for permission. But why? What is it about the most indifferent creature on the planet that makes humans absolutely lose their minds? Think black cats bring bad luck? Think again. The truth about black cats is stranger, richer, and way more interesting than the superstition and Caitlin and Clay are here to set the record straight. In this episode of Cat Cafe, America's favorite vet receptionist Caitlin Palmer and her cat daddy husband Clay Palmer dive deep into the wild world of cat mythology, feline folklore, and the weirdest cat superstitions that humans have carried for centuries. We are talking black cats across cultures — feared in some, worshipped in others. We are talking mythological cats from ancient Egypt to Norse legends to the shadowy corners of the internet. We are talking the real history behind the myths that still follow these animals into shelters today, where black cats consistently wait the longest for homes. Spoiler: the cats were never the problem. Think you know everything about cats? In this hilarious episode of Cat Cafe, America's favorite vet receptionist Caitlin Palmer takes on the ultimate cat trivia challenge — and her cat daddy husband Clay is putting her knowledge to the test. From quirky cat facts to surprising feline science, this quiz will challenge even the most devoted cat lovers. Play along and see if you can beat America’s favorite veterinary receptionist, Caitlin Palmer! But it's not just fun and games. Every wrong answer comes with a punishment — and that punishment is pickle juice. Yes, really. Watch to find out who walks away victorious and who walks away regretting their cat knowledge gaps. • Fun (and tricky) cat trivia questions • Surprising cat facts you probably didn’t know • A very questionable pickle juice challenge Who’s the ultimate cat nerd... and who’s about to drink pickle juice? In this hilarious episode of Pet Candy, Caitlin and Clay go head-to-head in a cat trivia challenge with a twist—get a question wrong, and you have to take a sip of pickle juice Think you know cats? Play along and see if you can beat them (without the punishment.) Every NAVLE Warrior asks some version of the same question during week six: am I studying the right way, or am I just studying the most? Cognitive science has a real answer to that question, and it is not the one most students expect Every NAVLE study plan is built around content: which species, which systems, which diagnoses to drill. But the brain that has to hold all of that information is a physical organ, and it runs on three inputs: sleep, movement, and nutrition. Neglect any one of them and the same number of practice questions will produce worse results. Here's the science behind why, and what to actually do about it. Starting with the October to November 2026 testing window, the NAVLE looks different in two ways that actually matter for how you study. The exam moved to a new block format back in the spring update, and now the ICVA has also refreshed the Species and Diagnosis list itself, adding more than 100 diseases across the species you'll be tested on. That is not a small revision. That is the blueprint growing, and it means the way you have been prepping needs a second look. Paid NAVLE prep services can cost more than $600 for a thirty month pass, sometimes more. For companies selling them, that is a subscription. For a fourth-year veterinary student, that can be groceries for two months. And in a year when gas prices and food prices have squeezed every budget in America, plenty of vet students are doing math far scarier than anything on the exam. There are continuing education programs, and then there are continuing education programs where you accidentally debunk a mythical creature between bites of fried dough. Tune in as we cover a promising breakthrough that could change the way we approach this aggressive cancer. Inside: Dr. Wailani Sung helps you learn how to Recognize the Subtle Signs of Pain in Cats. In this episode of Rounds with Dr. Shannon, Dr. Shannon Gregoire sits down with veterinary ophthalmologist Dr. DJ Haeussler for a real clinical conversation about the feline eye cases that challenge general practitioners the most, starting with the corneal ulcer that just won't close. A limping dog walks into your exam room. The owner says it started two weeks ago. The leg looks fine. The X-rays look fine. Nothing adds up — yet. In this episode of Mystery Case Rounds, Dr. Shannon Gregoire walks through a real clinical case of canine lameness from the first exam to the final diagnosis, showing exactly how she thinks through a case when the answer isn't obvious. Veterinary emergency specialist Dr. Kristin Welch walks through a real hyperglycemia case that didn't follow the textbook. Watch the diagnostic reasoning unfold on Vet Candy's Mystery Case Rounds. Roy Graber October 14, 2026 Article Summary Highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 was confirmed in a Peruvian laying hen flock in October, killing nearly 3,000 birds and forcing the depopulation of the remaining 2,860 hens, just over a month after the country had been declared free of the virus. H5N1 HPAI confirmed on October 7 in Centro Poblado El Tallán, Peru affecting a commercial laying hen flock 5,800 hens total: 2,940 died from infection and 2,860 were depopulated to control spread Infected birds showed respiratory and neurological signs before confirmation Outbreak occurred just over one month after Peru was declared H5N1-free on September 3 Response included quarantine measures, facility disinfection, and surveillance around the outbreak area Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) has been confirmed in a commercial laying hen flock in Centro Poblado El Tallán, Peru. According to a report from the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH), the case was confirmed Oct. 7. Of the 5,800 hens in the flock, 2,940 died and the remaining 2,860 were depopulated, the report said. The hens had exhibited respiratory and neurological signs. Once an H5N1 variant of HPAI was confirmed, the birds were stamped out, quarantine measures were taken and an epidemiological investigation was launched. The epidemiological unit was cleaned and disinfected, and surveillance was conducted around the outbreak to detect possible cases, WOAH said. The infection came just over a month after Peruvian poultry was declared free of H5N1 HPAI. The previous outbreak was resolved Sept. 3. WOAH also has active reports on HPAI in nonpoultry and wild birds in Peru, including one concerning the H5N1 subtype and another concerning an untyped H5 HPAI variant. WOAH has an active report on Newcastle disease in Peru as well, but that report has not been updated in more than a month. View our continuing coverage of the global avian influenza situation. Edited by: Damián Morais State agriculture officials quarantine two commercial dairies in Yakima County following the Pacific Northwest state’s first confirmed detections of H5N1 in cattle. The Washington State Department of Agriculture (WSDA) and the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) National Veterinary Services Laboratories have confirmed the state’s first cases of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) H5N1 in dairy cattle, placing two commercial dairy operations in Yakima County under mandatory quarantine. The confirmed detections expand the geographic reach of the bovine influenza outbreak, making Washington the twentieth U.S. state to identify H5N1 in dairy cattle since the cross-species transmission was first documented in early 2024. State and local health authorities, including the Yakima Health District, have activated clinical surveillance protocols to monitor exposed dairy workers and veterinary personnel. Public health officials emphasize that while human transmission risks remain low and pasteurized commercial milk supplies remain safe, immediate movement restrictions and enhanced biosecurity barriers are mandatory to contain localized spread. See also: Fonterra’s 25-year milk price legacy shaped by global market dynamics From an animal pathology and veterinary perspective, H5N1 manifestation in lactating dairy cattle presents a distinct clinical profile compared to the acute mortality observed in avian species. Affected cows typically exhibit sudden lethargy, diminished dry-matter feed intake, ruminal stasis, and a precipitous decline in daily milk yield. The raw milk produced by infected animals undergoes marked physical changes, turning into a thickened, yellow, colostrum-like secretion characterized by elevated somatic cell counts and high viral loads shed directly from mammary epithelial tissue. While mortality among adult cows remains low—with most animals regaining baseline health and partial lactation persistency over a two-to-three-week supportive therapy regimen—the disease inflicts temporary metabolic distress and significant milk solids losses. State veterinarians are requiring affected herds to isolate clinical animals, restrict milk disposal to prevent wildlife scavenging, and divert affected secretions away from the bulk tank. From a food safety and commercial processing standpoint, the confirmation of H5N1 within Washington’s raw milk shed does not compromise the commercial retail supply chain. Federal regulatory agencies, including the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the USDA, have repeatedly validated that commercial thermal pasteurization—whether High-Temperature Short-Time (HTST) or Higher-Heat Shorter-Time (HHST)—effectively inactivates influenza viruses, rendering store-bought fluid milk, cheese, and cultured products completely safe for human consumption. However, the presence of active viral shedding represents an acute health hazard for unpasteurized dairy consumption. Agricultural authorities have reissued strict public health warnings emphasizing that raw milk or unpasteurized dairy products derived from infected or unmonitored herds are unsafe for human or domestic animal consumption, highlighting that raw milk ingestion has historically driven fatal viral transmissions in farm cats and companion animals. The Yakima County detections introduce heightened operational and logistical friction across the Pacific Northwest dairy corridor, an intensive milk shed closely interconnected with neighboring Idaho and Oregon. Dairy co-operatives and private hauling operators must enforce rigorous sanitation protocols across bulk milk transport tankers, intake docks, and receiving bays to eliminate mechanical vector transfer between production sites. Furthermore, under federal animal health orders, producers transporting lactating dairy cows across state lines must conduct pre-movement testing through approved National Animal Health Laboratory Network (NAHLN) facilities. For farm managers, safeguarding production units requires implementing closed-herd protocols, restricting non-essential visitor access, establishing vehicle disinfection wheel baths, and equipping milking parlor personnel with personal protective equipment (PPE)—including eye protection, masks, and gloves—to prevent aerosol transmission during high-pressure parlor washdowns. See also: Western Star marks centenary with leading position in Australian butter market At the farmgate level, H5N1 quarantines impose direct balance sheet stress on commercial dairy operations. The combination of immediate milk yield losses, veterinary care expenditures, testing fees, and isolated disposal logistics quickly compresses operating margins. Although federal risk-mitigation programs—such as the USDA’s Emergency Assistance for Livestock, Honeybees, and Farm-Raised Fish Program (ELAP) and financial assistance for biosecurity implementation—provide partial indemnities for lost milk production and testing expenses, operational cash flows face disruption during quarantine periods. Sustaining disciplined biosecurity compliance and collaborating with state veterinary services will be critical for Pacific Northwest producers seeking to resolve active herd infections, lift quarantine orders, and protect herd asset value heading into 2027. (RFD-TV) — The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) is urging poultry and livestock producers to stay vigilant against highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) as fall bird migration begins. Cases declined during the summer months, but the seasonal movement of wild birds raises renewed concerns about the virus’s spread. USDA Under Secretary of Marketing & Regulatory Programs Dudley Hoskins says basic biosecurity practices remain essential to reducing transmission risks at agricultural facilities. “Think about clothing, think about your footwear, where you’ve been, washing your hands, what facility you may have been at that morning versus where you may be going that afternoon,” Hoskins said. “Anything you can do just to maintain vigilance and awareness of those kinds of fundamental principles is really what we’re asking people to do.” While poultry remains a primary concern, cattle producers are also monitoring the virus because dairy cattle are susceptible to HPAI. Hoskins says education and prevention efforts need to extend beyond farm operations. USDA’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service is working to mitigate the virus’s impact on American agriculture and producers. Hoskins says producers can help by educating employees, visitors, and people outside the farm gate about biosecurity practices. The current HPAI outbreak began in early 2022. USDA reports that approximately 31 million birds have been culled as part of the response. That figure does not mean every bird was confirmed to be infected, as depopulation may include birds exposed to the virus as part of disease-control efforts. One possible genetic clue is clade 2.3.2.1a, which was identified in poultry samples from the state in 2024. It was also detected in the virus that killed a two-year-old girl from Palnadu district in March 2025.Andhra Pradesh recorded two bird flu outbreak epicentres in February 2024, leading to the culling of about 300 birds. The scale increased sharply in 2025, when eight epicentres were reported across the state. More than 5.4 lakh birds died or were culled during those outbreaks in 2025.An older viral lineage:The National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (NIHSAD) identified clade 2.3.2.1a in poultry samples collected in Andhra Pradesh in 2024. At a World Organisation for Animal Health workshop in South Korea in August 2024, NIHSAD presented findings linking the samples to a lineage that has circulated in South Asia for several years.The same clade was identified in the virus detected in the Palnadu child. An H5N1 infection in an 11-year-old boy in Haryana in 2021 was also linked to this lineage. Research has additionally documented a human infection involving the broader clade 2.3.2.1 group in Nepal in 2019. by Taboolaby Taboola Sponsored LinksSponsored Links Promoted LinksPromoted Links You May Like Leave Some Honey Out For Your Dog Overnight, Here’s What HappensPets Daily Health Learn More Undo Genetic comparisons have shown similarities between viruses detected in India and Bangladesh, where clade 2.3.2.1a has circulated or re-emerged in poultry and other birds.A complex genetic history:The ICMR-National Institute of Virology in Pune analysed the Palnadu child’s specimen and submitted the genetic data to the Global Initiative on Sharing All Influenza Data (GISAID). The sequence belonged to clade 2.3.2.1a and clustered with a virus associated with an H5N1 infection reported in a child who fell ill while visiting Kolkata in 2024 and was diagnosed after returning to Australia.A study published in ‘Emerging Infectious Diseases’ found that the Australian virus was a reassortant, meaning its genome contained segments derived from different influenza virus lineages. Four gene segments, including the haemagglutinin segment, were most closely related to clade 2.3.2.1a viruses circulating in Bangladesh. Other segments showed relationships to viruses detected in Japan, South Korea and China, as well as to a low-pathogenicity avian influenza virus found in a duck in Taiwan.Segment-by-segment comparisons identified similarities with viruses from a duck in Wakayama, Japan; a white-fronted goose in South Korea; a duck in China; and a duck in Taiwan. Another comparison involved an environmental sample from Kagoshima, Japan.These findings relate to individual gene segments. They do not show that the complete virus passed sequentially through Bangladesh, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and China, nor do they establish how the infection reached Andhra Pradesh.Possible routes of introduction:Migratory wild birds can introduce avian influenza viruses into domestic poultry. Other possible routes include the movement of infected poultry, contaminated vehicles and equipment, contact between backyard and commercial birds, environmental contamination and gaps in biosecurity.The latest Anantapur outbreak warrants further investigation because the farm procured birds from Telangana, even though no fresh outbreaks had been reported there. Investigators will need to determine whether the birds were infected before arrival, whether the virus was introduced through subsequent contact, or whether it entered the farm through another route.Animal husbandry department joint director Dr Prem Chand said farmers had reported unusual bird deaths at poultry units operating under the National Livestock Mission in Anantapur. “Samples were sent to Vijayawada, where they initially tested positive for bird flu. The infection was subsequently confirmed by the laboratory in Bhopal. Poultry operations will remain suspended within a 1-km radius of the infected premises for three months. The area within a 10-km radius has been designated as a surveillance zone,” said Dr Prem Chand. records.content: The sweeter side of veterinary medicine Welcome to your new favorite place to grow in vet med. Discover brilliant experts, engaging videos, interactive quizzes, inspiring stories, and podcasts that keep you curious, connected, and excited about what's next. After serving in the U.S. Navy, raising a family while earning her veterinary degree, and drawing inspiration from her immigrant mother's entrepreneurial journey, Dr. Lieu Balu is preparing to lead her own veterinary clinic in Phoenix. Scientists detect H5 bird flu antibodies in apparently healthy Greenland polar bears, raising new concerns about wildlife disease spread in the Arctic. Ask most people what a veterinary pathologist does all day and they’ll probably picture microscopes, slides, cells, and very serious diagnostic reports. Dr. Aleksandra Zuraw certainly does all of that. New research involving nearly 900 dogs reveals that larger breeds don't just have shorter lives. Their bodies may actually age faster at the molecular level, and the discovery could change how scientists approach canine longevity. H5N1 bird flu strikes Minnesota turkey and Indiana duck farms as another Texas dairy herd tests positive, raising new concerns for veterinarians. LMU researchers challenge a decades-old model: genetically modified embryos lacking interferon tau can establish pregnancies and develop into healthy calves. A landmark Purina study found that lean Labrador Retrievers lived 1.8 years longer and developed chronic disease later. Here's why the findings still matter for veterinarians 25 years later. Scientists warn that emerging African swine fever variants could undermine vaccine protection, making surveillance and biosecurity more important than ever. Letter of Reasonable Assurance clears the way for Maryland’s first in-state veterinary school to begin recruiting and admitting its inaugural class in 2027 11 careers. 6 questions. Zero chill. Veterinary medicine isn't one job—it's about eleven careers hiding under the same white coat. There is a conversation happening in break rooms, group chats, and parking lots all over veterinary medicine. It usually starts the same way. I love the medicine, but I do not know how much longer I can do this. And it usually ends with a quiet assumption that something is wrong with the person saying it. Somewhere along the way, veterinary medicine developed an unwritten rule: clinical practice is the real job, and everything else is quitting. It gets absorbed in school, reinforced in practice, and carried around as guilt by veterinarians who are exhausted, curious, or simply ready for a change but afraid that stepping out of the exam room means abandoning their oath. If you are graduating this year, the offers are probably already arriving, and some of the numbers are eye-watering. Signing bonuses have become the headline of new grad recruitment, and with student debt where it is, nobody could blame you for reading the biggest number and reaching for a pen. Vet school can turn almost anything into a performance metric. Grades, class rank, clinical skills, productivity, sleep, exercise, and sometimes even food can quietly become one more thing you feel like you should be “doing right.” Add long days, irregular schedules, stress, limited money, constant comparison, and a culture that can reward pushing through discomfort, and it is easy for a complicated relationship with food or your body to hide in plain sight. There are queer and trans veterinarians who came before you, students at other schools experiencing many of the same things, peer-support volunteers willing to listen, community organizations that know your city, and national groups that can help when a problem becomes medical, legal, academic, or overwhelming. Vet school has a way of eating your entire calendar. Between exams, labs, rotations, boards, jobs, relationships, and trying to get enough sleep to remain functional, personal health can slide down the priority list pretty quickly. There is a particular kind of kitchen alchemy that happens when nothing gets thrown away: a roast chicken becomes dinner, then lunch, then the broth for Thursday's ramen. A single Sunday afternoon becomes a month of breakfasts. What follows is not a diet plan so much as a system, one built on a $500 monthly grocery budget, a single person's appetite, and the stubborn belief that homemade is both cheaper and better. Meet Mecca Gladney, a first-generation college graduate, mother, and University of Arizona veterinary student pursuing a career in veterinary surgery while championing representation, mentorship, and mental health. The UC Davis veterinary student took a winding road to her dream school, but every setback helped shape the veterinarian and mentor she hopes to become. Now Monika Lagarejos wants to use her place in veterinary medicine to care for animals, strengthen communities, and make sure the next generation of future veterinarians knows they belong. McPaul Hermoso started veterinary school at 35 after earning multiple degrees and living in five countries. Discover his unconventional journey, lifelong dream of becoming a veterinarian, and mission to inspire others. From four years cheering at LSU to studying veterinary medicine at the Royal Veterinary College, Jalyne Blackwell is building a career by saying yes to the opportunities that scare her a little—and trusting that the unexpected path might be the right one. After France’s competitive exams shut the door, this 20-year-old found her calling 800 miles from home — and proof that a detour can still lead exactly where you were meant to go. Meet Taja Bell, an LSU veterinary student, Army Animal Care Specialist, mom and model working toward a future in emergency medicine and surgery. There is a particular kind of courage it takes to walk away from a career you have already proven yourself in and start over as a first-year student. Emese Avdeyenkova has done exactly that, twice over, once when she traded a biology degree for an Army uniform, and again when she traded that uniform for a white coat. Now she is bringing all of it, the discipline, the humility, and the hard-won perspective, to Vet Candy Radio as one of the vet student hosts of Vet School After Dark. America's favorite vet receptionist Caitlin Palmer and her cat daddy husband Clay Palmer dig into the real science, history, and psychology behind humanity's longest-running obsession. We're talking ancient Egypt, where cats were literally worshipped as gods. We're talking the internet, where cats generate more content than almost anything else on the planet. From ancient worship to TikTok stardom, cats have clawed their way into our hearts and honestly, they never asked for permission. But why? What is it about the most indifferent creature on the planet that makes humans absolutely lose their minds? Think black cats bring bad luck? Think again. The truth about black cats is stranger, richer, and way more interesting than the superstition and Caitlin and Clay are here to set the record straight. In this episode of Cat Cafe, America's favorite vet receptionist Caitlin Palmer and her cat daddy husband Clay Palmer dive deep into the wild world of cat mythology, feline folklore, and the weirdest cat superstitions that humans have carried for centuries. We are talking black cats across cultures — feared in some, worshipped in others. We are talking mythological cats from ancient Egypt to Norse legends to the shadowy corners of the internet. We are talking the real history behind the myths that still follow these animals into shelters today, where black cats consistently wait the longest for homes. Spoiler: the cats were never the problem. Think you know everything about cats? In this hilarious episode of Cat Cafe, America's favorite vet receptionist Caitlin Palmer takes on the ultimate cat trivia challenge — and her cat daddy husband Clay is putting her knowledge to the test. From quirky cat facts to surprising feline science, this quiz will challenge even the most devoted cat lovers. Play along and see if you can beat America’s favorite veterinary receptionist, Caitlin Palmer! But it's not just fun and games. Every wrong answer comes with a punishment — and that punishment is pickle juice. Yes, really. Watch to find out who walks away victorious and who walks away regretting their cat knowledge gaps. • Fun (and tricky) cat trivia questions • Surprising cat facts you probably didn’t know • A very questionable pickle juice challenge Who’s the ultimate cat nerd... and who’s about to drink pickle juice? In this hilarious episode of Pet Candy, Caitlin and Clay go head-to-head in a cat trivia challenge with a twist—get a question wrong, and you have to take a sip of pickle juice Think you know cats? Play along and see if you can beat them (without the punishment.) Every NAVLE Warrior asks some version of the same question during week six: am I studying the right way, or am I just studying the most? Cognitive science has a real answer to that question, and it is not the one most students expect Every NAVLE study plan is built around content: which species, which systems, which diagnoses to drill. But the brain that has to hold all of that information is a physical organ, and it runs on three inputs: sleep, movement, and nutrition. Neglect any one of them and the same number of practice questions will produce worse results. Here's the science behind why, and what to actually do about it. Starting with the October to November 2026 testing window, the NAVLE looks different in two ways that actually matter for how you study. The exam moved to a new block format back in the spring update, and now the ICVA has also refreshed the Species and Diagnosis list itself, adding more than 100 diseases across the species you'll be tested on. That is not a small revision. That is the blueprint growing, and it means the way you have been prepping needs a second look. Paid NAVLE prep services can cost more than $600 for a thirty month pass, sometimes more. For companies selling them, that is a subscription. For a fourth-year veterinary student, that can be groceries for two months. And in a year when gas prices and food prices have squeezed every budget in America, plenty of vet students are doing math far scarier than anything on the exam. There are continuing education programs, and then there are continuing education programs where you accidentally debunk a mythical creature between bites of fried dough. This particular offering from Vet Candy lands firmly in the second category. Based on a short story by Vet Candy’s CEO and X-Files super fan, Dr. Jill Lopez. Dr. Joya Griffin and Dr. Forrest Cummings just dropped the veterinary CE series that changes how you think about complex cases and it is free with your Vet Candy membership. Free RACE-approved veterinary CE is now available on Vet Candy with Unleash Your Inner Hero! , an 8-module urgent care program led by veterinary criticalist Dr. Natosha Richardson. Offering 3.5 RACE CE credits for veterinarians and veterinary technicians, this course covers triage, CPR, supportive care, diagnostics, and treatment across neurologic, gastrointestinal, respiratory, and integumentary emergencies. Free RACE-approved veterinary CE is now available on Vet Candy with Dermatology Secrets featuring Dr. Joya Griffin. This three-part online course is designed for veterinarians and veterinary technicians and covers the dermatology skills that matter most in everyday practice — skin cytology, histopathology and biopsy interpretation, and the strangest and most diagnostically challenging cases in specialist dermatology. Learn how to read a cytology slide with confidence, decode a dermatopathology report, and work through complex skin presentations that have not responded to standard treatment. Earn 1.5 RACE CE credits at no cost with your free Vet Candy Membership! Free RACE-approved veterinary CE is now available on Vet Candy with the Respiratory Disease Master Course featuring Criticalist Dr. Anthony Gonzalez. Brought to you by Trudell Animal Health, this 8-module course provides 4 RACE CE credits for veterinarians and veterinary technicians. It covers recognition, diagnosis, and management of acute and chronic respiratory disease, including practical guidance on critical care, advanced monitoring, oxygen therapy, and evidence-based treatment strategies. Designed for immediate clinical application, this course helps veterinary professionals improve outcomes in high-stakes respiratory cases. Free RACE-approved veterinary CE is now available on Vet Candy with Endocrinology Secrets featuring Dr. Forrest Cummings. This online course is designed for veterinarians and veterinary technicians and covers real-world management of diabetes in dogs and cats, Cushing’s disease, and Addison’s disease. Learn how to interpret diagnostics, manage challenging endocrine cases, and improve patient outcomes with practical, case-based guidance. Earn 2 RACE CE credits at no cost—no subscription or credit card required. The Gut-Brain connection is more connected than we thought. This episode of Catching Up explores the fascinating link between the gut and brain in pets. Could your patient's GI issues be tied to behavior? The science says yes. Acute Kidney Injury Alert: New Biomarkers That Could Save Lives. Dr. Elan Armstrong & Dr. Shannon Gregoire break down the newest research on acute kidney injury. World-First Breakthrough: Stem Cells from Cats Could Revolutionize Kidney Disease Treatment! Vet Candy has the details with Dr. Elan & Dr. Shannon. Big news in hemangiosarcoma research! Tune in as we cover a promising breakthrough that could change the way we approach this aggressive cancer. Inside: Dr. Wailani Sung helps you learn how to Recognize the Subtle Signs of Pain in Cats. Presented by Zoetis, maker of Solensia. SolensiaVetTeam.com A cat eye that won't heal is one of those cases that can quietly spiral into something serious — fast. In this episode of Rounds with Dr. Shannon, Dr. Shannon Gregoire sits down with veterinary ophthalmologist Dr. DJ Haeussler for a real clinical conversation about the feline eye cases that challenge general practitioners the most, starting with the corneal ulcer that just won't close. A limping dog walks into your exam room. The owner says it started two weeks ago. The leg looks fine. The X-rays look fine. Nothing adds up — yet. In this episode of Mystery Case Rounds, Dr. Shannon Gregoire walks through a real clinical case of canine lameness from the first exam to the final diagnosis, showing exactly how she thinks through a case when the answer isn't obvious. Veterinary emergency specialist Dr. Kristin Welch walks through a real hyperglycemia case that didn't follow the textbook. Watch the diagnostic reasoning unfold on Vet Candy's Mystery Case Rounds. Dr. Ashley Bourgeois breaks down what is really going on when a Pomeranian loses its coat, the hormonal, genetic, and inflammatory factors may be at play, why this breed is uniquely predisposed to certain dermatologic conditions, and how to build a workup that actually leads somewhere instead of chasing your tail. Nearly a quarter of homeless youth in the U.S. have pets — and some choose veterinary care over their own health care. The Seattle One Health Clinic offers both, side by side, for free. Jeremiah Pouncy shares why this One Health model is changing how we think about the human-animal bond and community care. In Barcelona, scientists are building a biological deep freeze for endangered species, storing genetic material from nearly 300 species and using AI to unlock the future of conservation. Jeremiah Pouncy explains how the Barcelona CryoZoo could change everything we know about saving wildlife from extinction. With fewer than 800 left on Earth, the Bengal florican is one of the rarest birds alive. But in India's Manas National Park, over 800 former poachers have become the species' fiercest protectors. Jeremiah Pouncy tells the remarkable story of how community-led conservation turned a near-extinction into a comeback. A new study on the "Capitoline dolphins" off Rome's coast reveals a population in crisis. Seven out of ten show signs of malnutrition, many bear scars from fishing gear, and scientists warn they may disappear without urgent intervention. Jeremiah Pouncy breaks down what is threatening one of the world's most historically significant dolphin populations and why it matters. Going back to veterinary school usually means new classes, new rotations, new schedules, and the familiar feeling that summer disappeared way too fast. For the hosts of Vet School After Dark , it also means catching up on where everyone spent the break and figuring out how to mentally transition back into another demanding academic year. Vet Candy's hit podcast recently went live in Nashville, and what started as another fast-paced battle of veterinary knowledge quickly turned into something no one in the room saw coming. Dr. Lauren Downey Koos didn't have to look far to get to WVC Nashville. She works at BluePearl Veterinary in Franklin, Tennessee, which means the conference is essentially in her backyard. She graduated from the University of Florida in 2018, went into neurology, and became a specialist faster than most people finish paying off their student loans. Hosts Caitlin and Clay Palmer, the masterminds behind Vet Candy's trivia and news game show, challenge Carey to a fast-paced reckoning with the week's wildest veterinary headlines, most surprising research breakthroughs, and oddest animal stories circulating through the profession. It's loosely inspired by NPR's Wait Wait... Don't Tell Me, except everyone involved actually knows what a splenectomy is. Photo: PR IMAGE PHOTO Cases of a new strain of bird flu were always expected to reach Australia's shores at some point, with the disease now detected across two states. A South Australian wildlife rescue centre where a migratory bird tested positive for H5N1 bird flu remained in lockdown as of Thursday. It comes after the nation's first two confirmed cases were reported near Esperance in Western Australia. Wildlife experts believe it is only a matter of time before further bird flu outbreaks. (HANDOUT/Esperance Wildlife Hospital and Sanctuary) Advertisement Ad WA Premier Roger Cook said there was always an expectation the strain would arrive in Australia at some point but the country had an advantage in detecting the initial cases relatively early. "In other countries, it's got into their poultry industry before they even knew it was their area - so the fact that we've got these early lines of sight is really important," he told reporters on Thursday. "We're doing a lot of work with the industry at the moment around what they need to prepare themselves for and how they need to respond." WATCH: Everything you need to know about the H5N1 bird flu strain Advertisement Ad Volunteers from the Wildlife Welfare Organisation SA collected the first bird to test positive in that state from Knights Beach, roughly 80km south of Adelaide, on June 14. Rescue centre manager Justin Biddle said the team decided to send samples for testing after being alerted to the positive cases in Esperance. "It otherwise looked pretty fit and healthy and it was actually doing quite well in care," he told AAP. "We can't stop migratory birds from entering Australia," rescue centre manager Justin Biddle says. (Dean Lewins/AAP PHOTOS) Advertisement Ad Mr Biddle said there had been no noticeable increase in unwell birds beyond what the organisation generally expected, but more cases appeared inevitable. "We can't stop migratory birds from entering Australia - which is who's going to be carrying it - and it's this time of year where the migratory Antarctic birds start hitting the southern coastline of Australia," he said. Scientists warn the threat of a slew of wild birds becoming infected is "more when than if". "It may not spread in this winter, but it could come from shorebirds ... in the next summer," BirdLife Australia president Hugh Possingham said on Thursday. "It'll probably get here eventually ... that's unavoidable. "The way migratory birds are coming to this continent from other continents and other places - something is going to happen." Three cases of H5N1 bird flu have been detected - two in WA and one in SA. (Susie Dodds/AAP PHOTOS) Advertisement Ad There was currently no threat to humans, federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins confirmed. "Chicken meat and eggs, as prepared normally, are perfectly safe to eat," she said. WA authorities have received almost 200 reports of sick birds since the first suspected case. Authorities confirmed on Wednesday another case of the strain had been detected in a southern giant petrel at Quindalup on the South West coast, north of Margaret River. The preliminary positive result has yet to be officially confirmed and a sample has been sent for further testing. Ground-based surveillance and drone surveys are being conducted at sea lion breeding sites along the South Australian coast, with testing frequency increased in high-risk areas. A temporary ban on all poultry products imported from Australia, imposed by Papua New Guinea's National Agriculture and Quarantine Inspection Authority on Monday, has been lifted. Conditions Bird Flu Hits Indiana Duck Facility and Minnesota Turkey Farm as Another Texas Dairy Herd Tests Positive Published Oct 13, 2026 3:44 AM EDT By Elena Vega YURI TUTOV | AFP via Getty Images Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on Pocket H5N1 avian influenza has struck two large poultry operations in the Midwest and another dairy herd in Texas, according to the latest federal data. The U.S. Department of Agriculture reported six new detections in the past week, CIDRAP reported, including a commercial turkey farm in Stearns County, Minnesota, with 34,400 birds and a commercial duck meat facility in Jay County, Indiana, with 24,300 birds. Federal officials also confirmed H5N1 in another Texas dairy cattle herd. All three cattle detections reported nationwide in the past 30 days have been in Texas. Texas confirmed its first infected dairy herd of 2026 in late May, after cows at a farm became sick and milk production dropped, and the farm was quarantined. Dairy detections matter because infected cows shed large amounts of virus in milk, which raises the exposure risk for workers in milking parlors and is a key reason federal officials stress pasteurization. The risk to the general public remains low, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The people most affected are those who work closely with infected animals, along with households that keep backyard birds or drink raw milk. New Detections in Three States Minnesota remains the center of fall activity. The state has reported eight affected commercial flocks and three backyard flocks in the past 30 days, with 343,050 birds affected, according to the USDA's flock detection tracker as summarized by CIDRAP. Stearns County is in central Minnesota and is home to St. Cloud. Nationwide, about 550,000 birds in 12 commercial flocks and nine backyard flocks have been affected over the past 30 days. Infected flocks are typically culled to stop the virus from spreading to other farms. The Indiana detection adds a second Midwest state to this fall's list of large commercial outbreaks. Jay County, in east-central Indiana near the Ohio line, has faced bird flu before this year. The Commercial Review reported two earlier detections in the county in March, including one at a commercial breeder duck facility. MedicalDaily previously reported that three more Minnesota flocks tested positive for H5N1 as fall waterfowl migration carried the virus south. Those outbreaks in Big Stone, Becker and Otter Tail counties affected about 118,000 birds. The newest detections move the virus into central Minnesota and Indiana and show dairy infections continuing in Texas. Low Public Risk, Higher Risk on Farms No new human infections with novel influenza viruses were reported to the CDC in the week ending Oct. 3, according to the agency's FluView report. The CDC continues to describe the current public health risk from H5N1 as low. The risk is different for people who handle infected animals. Poultry workers, dairy workers, farm families, veterinarians, and people who help depopulate flocks have the most direct exposure to the virus through birds, manure, milk, and contaminated surfaces. Most U.S. human cases since 2024 have occurred in people with that kind of contact. Farm workers who develop eye redness or irritation, fever, cough, sore throat, or muscle aches within 10 days of exposure should contact a clinician or health department and mention their work. Prompt testing matters because antiviral treatment works best when started early, and it helps public health officials track any change in how the virus behaves. Cooking poultry and eggs to safe temperatures kills the virus, and pasteurization protects milk. After an earlier Texas dairy detection this year, the Texas Animal Health Commission said FDA is confident that pasteurization inactivates H5N1 and that "the commercial, pasteurized milk supply is safe," according to FOX 7 Austin. Household Precautions During Fall Migration Most households do not need to change their routines. The practical steps apply mainly to people with animals or farm connections. Backyard flock owners should keep birds away from wild waterfowl, limit visitors, and report sudden deaths or illness to their state veterinarian or the USDA. Raw, unpasteurized milk carries a higher risk of exposure to H5N1 and other germs. Pet owners should keep cats away from raw milk, raw pet food made from poultry, and dead birds, since cats have been infected through these routes in past outbreaks. People who find dead wild birds should not touch them with bare hands and can report them to state wildlife officials. Hunters handling waterfowl this season should wear gloves, avoid eating or drinking while dressing birds, and wash their hands thoroughly afterward. Anyone with flu-like symptoms after close contact with sick or dead birds or livestock should tell a clinician about the exposure. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, or confusion needs emergency care. Federal Reporting and What Comes Next The USDA updates its livestock detection map each weekday. Fall and spring typically bring more poultry detections because migrating wild birds carry the virus along their flyways. Officials have not said how the Texas dairy herd became infected or whether nearby herds are being tested. The source of the Indiana duck facility infection has also not been publicly identified. MedicalDaily will continue tracking new poultry and dairy detections, any human cases reported by state health departments, and any change in federal risk assessments. The USDA reported H5N1 at a Stearns County, Minnesota, turkey farm with 34,400 birds, a Jay County, Indiana, duck facility with 24,300 birds, and a Texas dairy herd. How many birds have been affected recently? About 550,000 birds in 12 commercial and nine backyard flocks have been affected nationwide in the past 30 days, including 343,050 in Minnesota. Is H5N1 a risk to the general public? The CDC says the current public health risk is low. No new human infections with novel flu viruses were reported in the week ending Oct. 3. Who faces the highest risk? Poultry and dairy workers, farm families, veterinarians, and people with backyard flocks or close contact with sick animals face the greatest exposure. Is it safe to eat turkey, chicken and eggs? Yes, when properly cooked. Cooking poultry and eggs to safe temperatures kills the virus, and pasteurization makes commercial milk safe. What symptoms should exposed workers watch for? Eye redness, fever, cough, sore throat, or muscle aches within 10 days of contact with infected animals should prompt a call to a clinician or health department. How can backyard flock owners protect their birds? Keep birds away from wild waterfowl, limit visitors, practice good hygiene and report sudden illness or deaths to state animal health officials. records.content: Sports Business News Life Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals ENVIRONMENT Jackie the Big Bear bald eagle died of bird flu, report finds Rene Ray De La Cruz USA TODAY NETWORK Oct. 15, 2026, 9:59 a.m. PT A post-mortem report revealed that the bald eagle Jackie died from a complex disease process. The primary cause of death was Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza, which led to a severe stomach ulcer. The ulcer caused internal bleeding, anemia, and a secondary bacterial infection. While an anticoagulant rodenticide was found in her system, it was not identified as the primary cause of death. The mystery surrounding the death of Jackie, one half of Big Bear Valley's famous bald eagle pair, has finally been answered. A newly released necropsy report found that Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza, commonly known as bird flu, was the primary underlying cause of the beloved eagle's decline and death. But wildlife experts say Jackie's case was unusual, involving a severe stomach ulcer, chronic blood loss, bacterial infection and multiple interconnected health problems that developed over time. The findings, released Wednesday by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance and Ojai Raptor Center, provide the most detailed explanation yet of what happened to the eagle known to millions of viewers who followed her life through Big Bear's popular nest cameras. What caused Jackie the Big Bear bald eagle to die? Veterinary pathologists determined Jackie was suffering from Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza, or HPAI, a virus that has circulated among wild bird populations across the United States in recent years. According to Steve Kubiski, director of disease investigations with the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, Jackie's case presented in an uncommon way. Rather than causing the typical symptoms associated with bird flu, the infection triggered a severe ulcer in her ventriculus, the muscular portion of a bird's stomach, or gizzard. The ulcer caused persistent internal bleeding that led to severe anemia and allowed bacteria to enter her bloodstream, resulting in bacterial sepsis. The report concluded those conditions, combined with widespread inflammation and blood clot formation, ultimately led to Jackie's death. Necropsy reveals chronic illness and internal bleeding The examination found evidence of a long-developing disease process involving significant damage to Jackie's stomach tissue. Wildlife veterinarians said the ulcerated tissue caused ongoing blood loss and persistent anemia. Testing also detected bird flu virus genetic material in multiple organs and tissues throughout her body, including the damaged stomach tissue. Researchers ruled out several other potential causes. Follow-up testing found Jackie was negative for West Nile virus, and heavy metals, including lead, were within acceptable limits and were not linked to her illness or death. The findings helped explain many of the symptoms wildlife specialists observed while Jackie was receiving treatment after she was found injured near the family's nest in Fawnskin in July. Was rat poison responsible for Jackie's death? Testing detected brodifacoum, a common anticoagulant rodenticide often used to kill rats and mice, in Jackie's liver. However, the necropsy found no signs of the uncontrolled bleeding typically associated with rodenticide poisoning. Because of that, investigators concluded brodifacoum was not the primary cause of illness or death, though the report noted the presence of the toxic substance and other environmental contaminants in her system. What the report means for California's bald eagles Wildlife officials say the findings could help biologists and veterinarians better understand how bird flu affects raptors and other protected species. "The necropsy results have helped connect many of the findings we were seeing throughout the eagle's hospitalization," Ojai Raptor Center Executive Director Chris Eksteen said in a statement. California Department of Fish and Wildlife Director Meghan Hertel said understanding Jackie's case may help inform future treatment and conservation efforts involving bald eagles and other wildlife exposed to avian influenza. The report also noted that the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's National Eagle Repository cremated Jackie's remains to reduce the risk of spreading bird flu to people or other wildlife. How are Shadow and the Big Bear eaglets doing? The report found no evidence that Shadow, Jackie's longtime mate, or their eaglets, Sandy and Luna, were sick. Since Jackie's death in August, Shadow has remained in the Big Bear area and has frequently been seen with a younger female bald eagle known as KD1, or Kaydee. Meanwhile, Sandy and Luna fledged earlier this year and entered the wild, giving a bright spot to thousands of eagle enthusiasts who followed the family online. records.content: 今日动态 生物通首页 今日动态 新技术专栏 人才市场 生物通首页 > 今日动态 > 正文 尼日利亚活禽市场H5N1与H9N2禽流感病毒的检出及其溢出与重配风险 时间:2026年10月12日 来源:BMC Veterinary Research 编辑推荐: 摘要 背景 禽流感病毒(AIVs)包括高致病性H5N1和低致病性H9N2,构成了重大的人畜共患威胁。自2006年和2017年分别在西非首次检测到这两种亚型以来,它们已多次传入尼日利亚。本研究旨在通过2022年3月至11月对尼日利亚Hadejia和Kano活禽市场(LBMs 广告 X 欢迎领域“高通量小分子筛选解决方案”>> 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 “畅读会员”登录查看原文链接 Research Open access 摘要背景禽流感病毒(AIVs)包括高致病性H5N1和低致病性H9N2,构成了重大的人畜共患威胁。自2006年和2017年分别在西非首次检测到这两种亚型以来,它们已多次传入尼日利亚。本研究旨在通过2022年3月至11月对尼日利亚Hadejia和Kano活禽市场(LBMs)的主动监测,调查这些病毒目前的遗传多样性及其溢出风险。结果我们采样了219只禽鸟,每只采集两份拭子(共438份拭子样本)。只要至少有一份拭子检测为阳性,即判定该只禽鸟为阳性。在禽鸟层面,在Kano Sabon Gari活禽市场的125只表面健康的珍珠鸡中检测到3只(2.4%)高致病性H5N1。值得注意的是,低致病性H9N2的检出率显著更高,Hadejia活禽市场的94只鸡中有10只(10.6%)阳性。总体而言,219只禽鸟中有13只(5.9%)H5N1或H9N2检测为阳性。系统发育和选择压力分析确认,H9N2病毒属于G1谱系,其血凝素(HA)基因中携带关键的哺乳动物适应性特征,包括S143T、S145T和S121T,这些位点与对类似人类的α2–6唾液酸受体亲和力增强相关。系统发育分析显示,该H5N1毒株归属于2.3.4.4b分支,与导致2021–2022年尼日利亚疫情以及2023年初尼日尔后续暴发的病毒株具有密切的遗传关系。结论在尼日利亚不同的活禽市场中检测到了H5N1和H9N2。尽管这些发现并未提供当前共同循环或基因重配的证据,但在更广泛的活禽市场体系中同时检测到这两种亚型,加之H9N2中存在的推定哺乳动物适应性标记,凸显了潜在的基因重配风险——一旦这些病毒日后在同一市场内共同循环并感染同一宿主,就可能发生重配。因此,需要持续进行基因组监测,以发现未来的病毒趋同和新兴重配毒株,并为大流行病应急准备和防控策略提供依据。 打赏 欢迎领取《CGT 研发全流程解决方案》 展开全文 开通VIP 享海量文章 全站开放获取+解锁超过 200万篇新闻全文+每日更新 2000+篇,学术前沿动态全时追踪! It is increasingly a practical framework for protecting profitability, reducing resource losses and securing the future of animal protein production. ADM’s approach aligns with its Next Generation Thinking strategy, which focuses on helping customers improve resource efficiency, production performance, and environmental outcomes. For animal nutrition professionals, sustainability can be viewed through 3 connected pillars: economic, environmental and social sustainability. Economic sustainability is the foundation of resilient production systems. A farm, integrator or feed business must remain profitable to continue investing in better practices, new technologies and long-term improvement. Feed cost efficiency, lower mortality, fewer downgraded products, improved feed conversion and longer productive lifespans all contribute directly to that objective. Environmental sustainability focuses on producing animal protein while using fewer natural resources and reducing pressure on land, water, air and biodiversity. In feed, this means improving nutrient efficiency, reducing nitrogen, phosphorus and mineral excretion, limiting avoidable waste and responsible sourcing raw materials. ADM supports these efforts through traceability and responsible sourcing programs aligned with its ambition to develop deforestation – and conversion – free supply chains, particularly in areas identified as having a greater risk of deforestation and ecosystem conversion. Social sustainability completes the picture by supporting safe, transparent and responsible food systems. It includes animal welfare, food safety, responsible use of resources, and the long-term viability of the people, farms and communities involved across the agricultural value chain. Starting with economics: The SINCRO treasure hunt ADM’s SINCRO service offering is based on a clear principle: progress must be measurable. The journey therefore begins with economic sustainability. By analysing technical and economic results, SINCRO helps identify where value is being lost and where growth opportunities can be captured. This is especially relevant in an industry where small performance gaps can translate into significant financial impact at farm or feed mill level. This approach can be compared to a treasure hunt. In many production systems, hidden losses are present in the data: a slightly higher feed conversion ratio, marginally increased mortality, downgraded eggs, reduced animal longevity, or inconsistent raw material quality. Individually, these gaps may appear limited. When converted into economic value, however, they can reveal substantial sources of lost profit. ADM illustrates this logic through digital tools such as TreasurePerform, which helps convert technical gaps versus a reference into economic losses. A difference in feed conversion ratio, mortality, laying persistency or egg discard rate can be expressed in monetary terms, making priorities easier to discuss and decisions easier to make. This first diagnostic step creates the basis for targeted actions, combining services, expertise and solutions to improve technical performance and strengthen economic sustainability. From grain to farm: A holistic route to environmental sustainability Raw material sourcing has a major influence on the carbon footprint of animal feed. Using verified deforestation-free raw materials can reduce deforestation-related supply chain risk and may lower certain environmental impacts associated with feed ingredient sourcing, depending on the sourcing scenario and assessment methodology. ADM supports customers with traceable sourcing solutions and responsible supply chain programs designed to reduce risks linked to deforestation and conversion. Its soy strategy included traceability, supplier engagement, risk assessment and monitoring aimed at reducing deforestation and land-conversion risks within high-risk sourcing regions. As customers increasingly seek to quantify the environmental impact of feed ingredients, access to credible life cycle assessment (LCA) data has become an important component of responsible sourcing. ADM offers products supported by Global Feed LCA Institute (GFLI)-branded life cycle assessment data, including soybean meal and palm kernel expeller, enabling customers to make more informed sourcing decisions and support transparent environmental reporting. For palm kernel expeller, this verified data demonstrates up to a 25% lower carbon footprint compared with conventional alternatives, illustrating how ingredient selection can contribute to measurable emissions reductions across both the feed supply chain and livestock production. Precision nutrition is another practical lever for improving sustainability. It helps nutritionists formulate closer to animals’ real requirements while limiting excess nutrients and avoidable waste. This starts with accurate characterization of raw materials, including their quality and variability. Through SINCRO, ADM helps customers access laboratory analyses and NIR calibrations to support their quality control programs. ADM’s MatrixNutri app supports this approach by converting analytical results for more than 400 ingredients into precise, species-specific nutritional values, including values for aquaculture and providing a robust foundation for accurate feed formulation. Together, these services are designed to help reduce resource losses associated with formulation variability while supporting profitability thereby supporting both environmental and economic goals. A practical example can be seen in a broiler trial conducted by ADM in which crude protein in the finisher diet was reduced from 19% to 16.2% in parallel to specific adjustments. Final live weight was maintained, while total protein intake decreased. In this trial, modelling indicated that the carbon footprint of the finisher feed was up to 17% lower than the reference formulation. At farm gate, modelling indicated lower environmental impacts per kg of meat produced for the indicators assessed in the study. This illustrates how ADM’s nutrition expertise can help customers move beyond least-cost formulation toward a broader optimization model that integrates economic, zootechnical, and environmental objectives. ADM’s broad portfolio of feed additives and specialty solutions complements its grain-to-farm approach by helping customers reduce production losses and improve resource efficiency and farm performance. Improving eggshell quality, for example, can reduce the number of downgraded or discarded eggs. Supporting laying hen longevity can reduce the non-productive investment represented by replacement pullets. Improving sow robustness and reproductive performance can reduce culling and save resources. Organic trace mineral solutions, such as the B-Traxim range, can support mineralbioavailability, thereby contributing to lower mineral excretion. In this context, ADM’s Next Generation Thinking strategy is not positioned as an opposition between profitability and sustainability. Rather, it shows that both objectives can reinforce each other when data, nutrition expertise and field performance are connected. By reducing technical gaps, improving nutrient use and animal robustness, limiting waste and supporting responsible raw materials sourcing, animal feed professionals can create more efficient production systems that are economically robust and designed to use resources more efficiently and reduce production losses. Conclusion: Building sustainable value through measurable improvement For the animal feed industry, the most effective sustainability strategies are those that can be measured, implemented and translated into value. ADM’s approach starts with economic performance because profitability gives producers the capacity to invest, adapt and improve. From there, SINCRO connects control of raw materials, precision nutrition and performance monitoring to help reduce variability and unlock hidden opportunities. ADM feed additives and specialty solutions provide another practical lever, helping improve nutrient efficiency, animal robustness, product quality and loss reduction across species and production systems. Actions that improve farm profitability, such as better feed efficiency, fewer losses, stronger animal robustness, longer productive lifespans and more accurate formulation, can also lower the use of natural resources. Responsible sourcing and traceability help address environmental risks associated with key raw materials, including land-use change and deforestation, before those materials enter the feed mill. This holistic model shows that sustainability is not a separate agenda for animal nutrition, but an integrated process supported by ADM at each step of the value chain. By combining sourcing expertise, analytical tools, nutrition services, performance monitoring and tailored solutions, ADM can help customers build more competitive, transparent and resilient production systems for the future.Learn more about ADM’s SINCRO solutions here. Some words may be mispronounced. BIG BEAR LAKE, Calif. (AP) — Bird flu caused the death of a bald eagle named Jackie who had become an internet sensation and a symbol of the species' recovery in California, officials said. A necropsy and additional testing found that the primary underlying cause of Jackie's death in August was highly pathogenic avian influenza, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife said Wednesday in a news release. In the weeks before she died, Jackie was being treated at the Ojai Raptor Center for various ailments, including anemia. Chris Eksteen, the center's director, said in the news release that the necropsy results “have helped connect many of the findings” they saw during her hospitalization. “In an uncommon presentation of the virus, the infection caused a severe ulcer in her stomach that led to persistent internal bleeding, anemia, and the development of bacterial sepsis," Steve Kubiski, the disease investigations director at the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, where the necropsy was conducted, said in the news release. For more than a decade, nature lovers watched via an online video feed as Jackie and her partner, Shadow, tended to their nest each year atop trees near Big Bear Lake in the San Bernardino Mountains east of Los Angeles. There's no evidence Shadow is ill, according to the news release. The nonprofit Friends of Big Bear Valley installed the nest camera in 2015 and documented the successes and failures of each breeding season. Highly pathogenic avian influenza has been circulating in bird populations throughout the U.S. While waterfowl and shorebirds are natural hosts for bird flu viruses, eagles and other raptors can be exposed through contact with infected birds or by eating them, according to the news release. Jackie's remains were cremated to prevent transmission of the virus, it said. American bald eagles teetered on the brink of extinction until the pesticide DDT was banned in the 1970s and other protections were established, leading the species to rebound and be removed from the federal endangered list. CA 30 of 30 News Avian Influenza identified as primary underlying cause of Big Bear bald eagle Jackie’s decline Credit: The Ojai Raptor Center Jackie the bald eagle at the Ojai Raptor Center (7/29/26) By Jesus Reyes October 14, 2026 6:43 PM Published October 14, 2026 6:11 PM BIG BEAR, Calif. (KESQ) - The final necropsy report on Jackie the Big Bear bald eagle's death was released on Wednesday, revealing Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza as the underlying primary cause of her decline. "The necropsy, performed by veterinary pathologists at the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, along with extensive additional laboratory and toxicology testing, provided new information about the complex medical condition that led to Jackie’s decline and death," reads a news release by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW). Jackie died on August 10 after more than three weeks of intensive medical care at the Ojai Raptor Center. Officials said the "necropsy revealed a complex and unusual disease process involving severe, chronic inflammation and ulceration of the stomach, persistent internal bleeding, anemia and secondary bacterial sepsis." Further diagnostic testing confirmed Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) within the affected tissues. HPAI is an infectious disease that primarily affects birds and has been circulating in wild bird populations throughout the United States, the CDFW reports. Waterfowl and shorebirds are natural hosts of avian influenza viruses, while eagles and other raptors may be exposed through contact with infected birds or by consuming infected prey. Officials identified HPAI as an underlying cause of Jackie's severe stomach ulceration. Multiple complications developed over time and ultimately contributed to her decline and death. "Jackie's necropsy confirmed Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) as the primary underlying cause of her decline," said Steve Kubiski, Director of Disease Investigations, San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance. "In an uncommon presentation of the virus, the infection caused a severe ulcer in her stomach that led to persistent internal bleeding, anemia, and the development of bacterial sepsis." The agency added that Jackie showed signs of chronic disease involving the ventriculus, the muscular portion of a bird’s stomach, commonly called the gizzard. The damaged and ulcerated tissue contributed to ongoing blood loss and her persistent severe anemia. It also allowed bacteria to enter the body, resulting in a serious secondary bacterial infection. Severe inflammation and blood clot formation were also found in the heart and several major blood vessels. Follow-up testing showed that HPAI virus genetic material was present in several tissues throughout her body, including the ulcerated tissue in the ventriculus. Together, the findings showed that Jackie was suffering from multiple severe and interconnected disease processes that had been developing over time and ultimately led to her decline and death. “The necropsy results have helped connect many of the findings we were seeing throughout the eagle’s hospitalization,” said Chris Eksteen, Executive Director of Ojai Raptor Center. “We are grateful to the many veterinary specialists, laboratories, wildlife agencies and partner organizations who worked alongside our team to understand her illness and provide her with the best possible care. Caring for her was an extraordinary privilege for our entire team.” Consistent with established procedures intended to prevent the transmission of HPAI to wildlife or humans, Jackie's remains were cremated by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s National Eagle Repository. A ministry team inspecting falcons kept in a veterinary center in Riyadh, which takes care of the birds that are usually used for hunting, discovered the cases, Saudi Press Agency quoted the ministry statement as saying. The ministry said the 37 falcons, including the five positive cases “were killed and burned.” Laboratory tests are being conducted to establish if the cases also test positive for the N virus — “the other component of the (bird flu) virus,” it added. In November the Kingdom banned all bird imports from neighboring countries. That decision came a day after Kuwait announced a bird stricken with avian flu in the country carried the deadly H5N1 strain, in the first case of its kind in the Gulf. Another bird was found to have the milder H5N2 strain. Scientists fear that the more the virus spreads, the greater the chance that H5N1 will mutate into a form that is easily transmissible between humans, making it capable of sparking a global pandemic that could claim millions of lives. The toll from the H5N1 strain of bird flu has climbed to 80 people worldwide since 2003. For a workers’ compensation case to be valid, you generally need: (1) to be a covered employee, (2) an injury/illness tied to your work, (3) timely notice to your employer and filing, and (4) medical proof that work caused or aggravated the condition. A causal link exists between the work and the injury or the worsening of a preâexisting condition (direct cause, aggravation, acceleration, or precipitation). records.content: Home latest pakistan world sports showbiz entertainment Royal business health Sci-Tech Food Fact Check Sci-Tech Videos shows Watch LIVE TV X Home Latest Pakistan World Sports Showbiz Fact Check Sci-Tech Videos Shows LIVE TV Viral Jackie the bald eagle died from avian influenza, California wildlife officials confirm Jackie, the bald eagle, died after a three-week health scare on August 10, 2026 By Web Desk | Published October 15, 2026 Jackie the bald eagle died from avian influenza, California wildlife officials confirm Jackie, the beloved bald eagle, whose cause of death has been revealed two months after her death in August. Jackie, who captivated millions online via a livestream of the aerie overlooking Big Bear Lake, shared with mate Shadow. The California Department of Fish and Wildlife has announced Jackie’s cause of death. The wildlife department on Wednesday, October 14, revealed that Jackie died from highly pathogenic avian influenza, also known as bird flu. Steve Kubiski, Director of Disease Investigations, San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, who performed the necropsy, said, “Jackie’s necropsy confirmed Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) as the primary underlying cause of her decline.” The infection caused a severe ulcer in her stomach that led to persistent internal bleeding, anaemia, and the development of bacterial sepsis,” Kubiski determined. Testing revealed that rat poison was in her system, but officials ruled it out as the primary cause of her illness or death. She had been suffering from multiple diseases, according to the department. Jackie, the bald eagle, died after a three-week health scare on August 10, 2026. The bald eagle, Jackie, raised multiple eaglets in Big Bear Lake with her partner Shadow, living a life for 14 years. Jackie was hatched from an egg in 2012, near Bug Bear Lake, California. She is survived by Shadow and her last two chicks, Luna and Sandy, who was born in March. Jackie’s long-time mate, Shadow is reportedly in good health and remains in Big Bear, according to the statement issued by the Fish and Wildlife department.
