records.content: ___ × Market Information Top Poultry Companies Expert Insights Blogs Regions Magazines Sign In Poultry Meat Egg Poultry Health Sustainability Poultry Future Chicken Marketing Summit Poultry Tech Summit Broilers & Turkeys Diseases & Health Avian Influenza Avian flu cases confirmed in poultry in 5 European states As the northern hemisphere fall reaches its peak, a handful of new outbreaks of highly pathogenic avian influenza involving domestic birds have been reported, while further infections in the wild population have been detected more widely across Europe. Jackie Linden October 12, 2026 mashi_naz | Bigstock Article Summary Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) outbreaks involving H5 viruses have been confirmed in poultry across five European countries—Belgium, Bulgaria, France, Germany, and the United Kingdom—over the past month, with hundreds of thousands of birds affected and 316 total farm outbreaks reported across Europe in 2026. Five European nations have confirmed HPAI outbreaks in poultry involving H5 family viruses since September 2026 Bulgaria reported 41,000 affected birds across two farms, bringing the nation's 12-month total to 18 outbreaks 2026 European totals show 316 poultry outbreaks in 16 countries, compared to 729 outbreaks across 23 countries in all of 2025 H5N1 virus variant dominates confirmed cases, with Poland leading at 143 outbreaks, followed by Germany with 40 Wild bird infections continue spreading with 2,709 HPAI outbreaks logged across Europe in 2026, primarily involving H5N1 Over the past month, new outbreaks of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in poultry involving viruses of the H5 family have occurred in Belgium, Bulgaria, France, Germany and the United Kingdom (U.K.). In Bulgaria, the H5N1 HPAI virus serotype has been detected at two more poultry farms in the central province of Plovdiv since mid-September, based on notifications to the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH). Affected at the first premises were 8,000 mallard ducks, followed by around 33,000 laying hens at the second location in the first week of October. These bring the nation’s total over the past 12 months to 18. Also confirming to WOAH two recent infections with this virus variant was France. Both those affected were commercial flocks in the department of Maine-et-Loire, and started in the first week of September. The first involved 2,500 vaccinated ducks, and the second close to 10,000 breeding ducks that had not been vaccinated against HPAI. Three French outbreaks have been reported since the end of August, all in Maine-et-Loire, which is located in the western region of Pays de la Loire. Great Britain’s HPAI outbreak total in poultry has increased to 20 following the detection of the H5N5 virus in the first days of October. Testing positive was a small backyard flock on the Isle of Lewis, according to the same source. Part of the Western Isles, Lewis is located off the northwestern coast of Scotland. Meanwhile, the veterinary authorities of Belgium and Germany have each reported to WOAH outbreaks linked to the H5N1 virus in captive birds. The Belgian outbreaks affected around 450 birds in mixed flocks in the Limburg and Antwerp areas, while the German outbreak in the northeast of the country is reported retrospectively, having started in May. Farm outbreak total approaches 320 So far in 2026, 16 countries in the region have confirmed a total of 316 HPAI outbreaks in poultry, according to the latest update of the Animal Disease Information System from the European Commission (EC; as of October 7). The database monitors listed animal diseases in European Union member states and selected adjacent countries (but not Great Britain). At each of the affected premises this year, presence of the H5N1 virus variant has been confirmed. For comparison, 729 outbreaks in these flocks were reported by 23 countries during the whole of 2025. This year, Poland’s total remains the highest to date at 143 although it has not changed since May. Next come Germany (40) and France (23). Including backyard poultry, ornamental flocks, zoos, and similar premises, the EC’s System monitors HPAI cases in “captive birds” in a separate category. To date in 2026, 15 countries have notified the System of 123 outbreaks involving captive birds. During the whole of last year, 25 countries registered 175 outbreaks in this category with the EC. HPAI-related developments affecting Europe’s poultry sector Based on the changing HPAI situation in the region, Germany’s veterinary reference laboratory Friedrich-Loeffler Institute has raised the disease risk level for the nation’s poultry flocks. The risk is now seen as “moderate” for both the transmission of H5 viruses to poultry and captive birds directly or indirectly from the wild population, and between wild birds within the country. Last month, EU member states agreed with a proposal from the European Commission Directorate for Agriculture, DG Agriculture and Rural Development (DG-AGRI) to release funds from the agricultural reserve to compensate Italian farmers hit by previous HPAI outbreaks. EUR61 million (US$68 million) will be directed to poultry and egg farmers whose businesses were impacted by measures taken to control and prevent the spread of infection between September of 2022 and March of 2025. Payments must be made to the recipients by May of next year. More widespread HPAI cases in wild birds As of October 7, a total of 2,709 HPAI outbreaks in Europe’s wild population had been logged by the EC’s System by 33 countries in 2026. Of these, the H5N1 virus serotype was involved in around 2,660, while the rest were identified as belonging to the H5 group. Based on EC data, wild birds infected with the H5N1 variant have been recorded by Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden over the past month. Following a hiatus of around 18 months, the same virus was detected again on the Mediterranean island of Cyprus in September, according to a recent WOAH notification. The same agency has been notified about the first wild birds that have tested positive for H5N1 since the start of the HPAI “season.” Six birds were found dead at four locations in England. Over the past month, WOAH has been informed about seven wild birds in Iceland that have tested positive for the H5N5 virus serotype. Please reference surfaced articles to validate AI summary Explore DeeperDive Full Summary Jackie, a 14-year‐old bald eagle from Big Bear Lake, California, died in August 2026 after an atypical case of highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1), leading scientists to label her infection a “scientific mystery.” The mysterious death of Jackie, a beloved California bald eagle, has been blamed on complications from avian influenza, news that has left some experts puzzled. "Nobody knew this was even a probability," said Dr. William Bowerman. "Her case gave us more science than we were expecting." Among the oddities: The disease wasn't believed to be widely circulating, said Bowerman, a professor of wildlife ecology and environmental toxicology at the University of Maryland who has been studying bald eagles since the 1980s. Officials announced Oct. 14 that a necropsy performed on Jackie, who died in August after a weekslong illness that mystified her doctors, revealed "Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) as the primary underlying cause of her decline," said Steve Kubiski, director of disease investigations for the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance. Jackie lived in Big Bear Lake in Southern California and was about 14 years old when she died. For the past decade, a camera livestreaming her nest captured major moments in her life, including laying eggs, raising eaglets and coupling up with mate Shadow. The result of the necropsy was a surprise to experts closely following Jackie's case, said Bowerman. The highly virulent strain of bird flu H5N1, which spread around the world in birds among migratory pathways, was first documented to be wiping out American bald eagles in 2022, causing numerous deaths and nest failures. The virus is still circulating and can infect wild birds, including raptors like the bald eagle, but there isn't a widespread outbreak as of late 2026, Bowerman said. That's good news for bald eagles, but the toll from the outbreak on the overall population level of the once endangered species is still untold, he said. Just how Jackie contracted HPAI is "another scientific mystery," Bowerman said. How did Jackie get bird flu? The reason it was so surprising that Jackie had bird flu is because her illness didn't present with typical symptoms, Bowerman said. Symptoms in an eagle might include walking in circles, holding and moving its head unnaturally, and being unable to fly, the National Park Service said. "In an uncommon presentation of the virus, the infection caused a severe ulcer in her stomach that led to persistent internal bleeding, anemia, and the development of bacterial sepsis," Kubiski said in an Oct. 14 summary of Jackie's necropsy. Also, there has been no active outbreak of bird flu in the area, according to Bowerman. Usually, obvious symptoms or multiple deaths of birds would be observed to signify H5N1 is sickening birds. "When you take a look up in Southern California, there was no outbreak of bird flu this year that they were seeing. California in the spring declared that it was no longer an impact to the poultry industry. So you would not expect that bird flu would have been the cause for her decline just based on her symptoms," Bowerman said. The necropsy would not have determined how she got it. Because it was an unusual presentation, it's not even clear when she may have been exposed. Bowerman said she could have gotten the virus in 2026, and a change in the disease progression caused it to appear differently, or she could have gotten it years earlier and it could have been lying dormant in her system until it flared up. How does bird flu spread in bald eagles? There are three main ways bald eagles and other raptors are thought to contract bird flu, according to Bowerman. They are: Drinking water containing bird poop with the virus. Spread between bald eagles in close proximity through inhalation. Preying on waterfowl such as duck and geese that are infected, or consuming birds that have died of it. This is thought to be a primary cause for bald eagles. Jackie may have eaten an infected duck or goose at some point. What Jackie's illness, death taught scientists Jackie was first taken from Big Bear Valley for treatment at the Ojai Raptor Center in July after she was seen in an altercation with other eagles. She was in critical condition but staff didn't know why. She first appeared underweight, with severe anemia and inflammation affecting her kidneys. Her medical team turned to several potential causes: lead poisoning, zinc toxicity, rodenticide poisoning, cancer. At one point she underwent a blood transfusion. "You would not have suspected bird flu," Bowerman said. In some ways, Jackie's unique illness and death has provided her medical team and scientists who study bird flu and bald eagles much more data to consider than any other eagle that has died from it, he said. That's because in a typical presentation of H5N1-caused demise, a bird would quickly be tested for the virus and immediately cremated upon a positive result. Though there hasn't been documented spread human-to-human, there is a chance the virus could mutate to enable such spread, so cremating the remains of infected birds ensures the risk of transmission is low. But because H5N1 wasn't an immediate suspected cause, many other tests and treatments were performed on Jackie that would not have been done on other birds, Bowerman said. records.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, October 15, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Cancer Breast milk-derived antibody preparation shields mice from influenza infection by October 15, 2026 in Cancer Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Breast milk-derived antibody preparation shields mice from influenza infection Filter Content Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A purified antibody preparation derived from pooled human breast milk has demonstrated broad antiviral activity in laboratory assays and meaningful protection against influenza in mouse models, according to a new study published in Science Advances. The product, known as LCTG-001, is a polyclonal secretory immunoglobulin A, or secretory IgA, preparation purified from breast milk collected from 120 donors through milk banks in Indianapolis and Pittsburgh. Yona Tugg and colleagues report that the preparation neutralized several medically important respiratory viruses in vitro, including respiratory syncytial virus, human adenovirus type 5, and both H1N1 and H3N2 strains of influenza A virus, raising the prospect of a mucosally delivered passive immunization strategy built from a renewable human biological resource. Secretory IgA occupies a distinctive position in the immune system’s defensive architecture. Unlike the circulating IgG that dominates blood-borne immunity, secretory IgA is the principal antibody class at mucosal surfaces, where most respiratory viruses first make contact with host tissue. It is produced locally by plasma cells in mucosal-associated lymphoid tissues and is transported across epithelial barriers by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor, which attaches a secretory component that stabilizes the molecule in the harsh enzymatic environment of the airway lumen. This dimeric, secretory-component-bearing structure allows secretory IgA to trap viruses in mucus, cross-link them at the epithelial surface, and neutralize them before they gain access to target cells. Because breast milk is a naturally enriched source of secretory IgA tuned by the maternal immune system’s extensive history of mucosal exposures, pooled milk represents a uniquely diverse polyclonal antibody repertoire. The breadth of activity observed in the new study reflects that diversity. In neutralization assays, LCTG-001 inhibited RSV, human adenovirus type 5, and two antigenically distinct influenza A subtypes, H1N1 and H3N2. The preparation also bound proteins and virus-like particles derived from H5N1 avian influenza viruses belonging to clade 2.3.4.4b, the lineage responsible for ongoing outbreaks in dairy cattle and sporadic human infections. Binding, however, did not translate into potent neutralization: against the H5N1 strain tested, LCTG-001 showed little neutralizing activity, and the authors did not test whether the preparation could protect animals against H5N1 challenge. The result illustrates a common distinction in antibody virology, where attachment to viral antigens does not necessarily correspond to functional inhibition of infectivity. Get Cold Relief Discover more Study Biology Get Cold Relief Track Pregnancy Pamper Your Baby Get Fresh Dairy The central in vivo experiments used mouse models of H1N1 influenza infection. Animals received two intranasal doses of LCTG-001, one administered two hours before infection and a second given 24 hours after exposure, a schedule designed to establish antibody at the mucosal surface both before viral entry and during the early phase of replication. Treated mice in both immunocompetent and antibody-deficient backgrounds experienced reduced illness and less lung damage than untreated controls. The protective effect in antibody-deficient mice is particularly notable, because it demonstrates that the exogenously delivered IgA can function without support from the recipient’s own humoral immune system, a property directly relevant to patients with primary or secondary antibody deficiencies who cannot mount robust antibody responses to vaccination. Get Cold Relief An intriguing pattern emerged from the virological measurements in immunocompetent mice. Lung viral loads were lower in treated animals early in infection, consistent with direct neutralization of inoculum virus at the respiratory mucosa, but by later time points the viral loads in treated and control mice were comparable. Despite this convergence in viral burden, treated animals retained less lung damage and better lung barrier integrity throughout. The authors suggest several non-mutually-exclusive explanations for this dissociation between viral load and pathology. Early neutralization may reduce the initial burst of replication and the inflammatory cascade it triggers, setting the disease trajectory on a milder course even if residual virus eventually replicates to similar levels. Alternatively, IgA-mediated immune complex formation may redirect antiviral responses toward less tissue-destructive pathways, or the antibody may directly modulate inflammatory signaling at the mucosal surface. Discover more Milk Filter Content Shop Grooming Two additional laboratory observations may bear on the mechanism of protection, although their in vivo contribution remains unresolved. First, LCTG-001 inhibited influenza neuraminidase activity in vitro. Neuraminidase, the surface glycoprotein targeted by the antiviral drugs oseltamivir and zanamivir, cleaves sialic acid residues and facilitates the release of newly formed virions from infected cells; antibody-mediated inhibition of this enzyme could plausibly slow viral spread within the lung. Second, when complexed with influenza antigens, LCTG-001 stimulated human neutrophils in vitro, hinting at a capacity to engage innate effector cells through Fc-dependent mechanisms. Polyclonal IgA immune complexes are known to interact with Fc-alpha receptors on neutrophils and other myeloid cells, and such interactions can promote phagocytosis or antiviral effector functions. Whether either of these activities contributes measurably to the protection observed in mice is a question the authors flag for future work. Get Cold Relief The therapeutic concept underlying LCTG-001 is mucosal passive immunization, the direct delivery of ready-made antibodies to the respiratory tract rather than relying on the recipient to generate them through infection or vaccination. Passive immunization with monoclonal antibodies has become an established paradigm for several infectious and immunological indications, but most approved products are administered systemically and target a single antigen. A polyclonal secretory IgA preparation delivered intranasally offers a different profile: it acts at the portal of viral entry, it carries specificity against many epitopes simultaneously, and its polyclonal composition may reduce the risk that viral escape mutations abolish protection, since a virus would need to alter multiple antigenic sites at once to evade the full antibody mixture. The donor pool is central to that breadth. The 120 donors whose milk fed the preparation carry antibodies shaped by decades of infections and vaccinations across genetically diverse immune systems, effectively compressing a population-level antibody repertoire into a single therapeutic lot. Milk banking infrastructure, already established for neonatal nutrition, provides a practical collection channel, although scaling production to a level suitable for widespread seasonal or pandemic use would pose substantial manufacturing, standardization, and regulatory challenges that the current study does not address. The researchers position LCTG-001 as a candidate for two distinct applications. The first is prophylaxis and early treatment for individuals with antibody deficiencies, a population in which influenza and other respiratory viruses can cause severe, prolonged disease and in which vaccine responses are often blunted. For these patients, an intranasal product that works independently of the recipient’s B-cell function could fill an important gap. The second, more speculative application is broader public health use, either as a complement to seasonal vaccination or as a rapidly deployable countermeasure during the early phase of an influenza pandemic, when a matched vaccine is not yet available and a polyclonal preparation with activity against multiple subtypes could bridge the interval. The binding observed against H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b antigens, even without strong neutralization, suggests the donor repertoire contains antibodies to avian influenza determinants, though the functional significance of that binding remains to be established. Important caveats frame the findings. All in vivo results come from mice, and the dosing schedule used in the animal studies was tightly controlled, with antibody delivered both before and shortly after infection; real-world performance under less predictable exposure conditions is unknown. No human efficacy data exist, and the authors are explicit that efficacy in humans has not been established. The mechanisms linking early viral load reduction and preserved lung integrity to the observed clinical benefit, as well as the roles of neuraminidase inhibition and neutrophil stimulation, remain open questions. Nevertheless, the study provides a proof of concept that a polyclonal secretory IgA product purified from pooled human breast milk can deliver broad antiviral activity at the mucosal surface and protect against influenza-induced illness and lung injury in animal models, establishing a foundation for the further preclinical and, eventually, clinical evaluation of breast milk-derived antibodies as mucosal therapeutics for respiratory viral disease. records.content: ___ × Market Information Top Poultry Companies Expert Insights Blogs Regions Magazines Sign In Poultry Meat Egg Poultry Health Sustainability Poultry Future Chicken Marketing Summit Poultry Tech Summit Broilers & Turkeys Diseases & Health Avian Influenza Avian flu cases confirmed in poultry in 5 European states As the northern hemisphere fall reaches its peak, a handful of new outbreaks of highly pathogenic avian influenza involving domestic birds have been reported, while further infections in the wild population have been detected more widely across Europe. Jackie Linden October 12, 2026 mashi_naz | Bigstock Article Summary Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) outbreaks involving H5 viruses have been confirmed in poultry across five European countries—Belgium, Bulgaria, France, Germany, and the United Kingdom—over the past month, with hundreds of thousands of birds affected and 316 total farm outbreaks reported across Europe in 2026. Five European nations have confirmed HPAI outbreaks in poultry involving H5 family viruses since September 2026 Bulgaria reported 41,000 affected birds across two farms, bringing the nation's 12-month total to 18 outbreaks 2026 European totals show 316 poultry outbreaks in 16 countries, compared to 729 outbreaks across 23 countries in all of 2025 H5N1 virus variant dominates confirmed cases, with Poland leading at 143 outbreaks, followed by Germany with 40 Wild bird infections continue spreading with 2,709 HPAI outbreaks logged across Europe in 2026, primarily involving H5N1 Over the past month, new outbreaks of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in poultry involving viruses of the H5 family have occurred in Belgium, Bulgaria, France, Germany and the United Kingdom (U.K.). In Bulgaria, the H5N1 HPAI virus serotype has been detected at two more poultry farms in the central province of Plovdiv since mid-September, based on notifications to the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH). Affected at the first premises were 8,000 mallard ducks, followed by around 33,000 laying hens at the second location in the first week of October. These bring the nation’s total over the past 12 months to 18. Also confirming to WOAH two recent infections with this virus variant was France. Both those affected were commercial flocks in the department of Maine-et-Loire, and started in the first week of September. The first involved 2,500 vaccinated ducks, and the second close to 10,000 breeding ducks that had not been vaccinated against HPAI. Three French outbreaks have been reported since the end of August, all in Maine-et-Loire, which is located in the western region of Pays de la Loire. Great Britain’s HPAI outbreak total in poultry has increased to 20 following the detection of the H5N5 virus in the first days of October. Testing positive was a small backyard flock on the Isle of Lewis, according to the same source. Part of the Western Isles, Lewis is located off the northwestern coast of Scotland. Meanwhile, the veterinary authorities of Belgium and Germany have each reported to WOAH outbreaks linked to the H5N1 virus in captive birds. The Belgian outbreaks affected around 450 birds in mixed flocks in the Limburg and Antwerp areas, while the German outbreak in the northeast of the country is reported retrospectively, having started in May. Farm outbreak total approaches 320 So far in 2026, 16 countries in the region have confirmed a total of 316 HPAI outbreaks in poultry, according to the latest update of the Animal Disease Information System from the European Commission (EC; as of October 7). The database monitors listed animal diseases in European Union member states and selected adjacent countries (but not Great Britain). At each of the affected premises this year, presence of the H5N1 virus variant has been confirmed. For comparison, 729 outbreaks in these flocks were reported by 23 countries during the whole of 2025. This year, Poland’s total remains the highest to date at 143 although it has not changed since May. Next come Germany (40) and France (23). Including backyard poultry, ornamental flocks, zoos, and similar premises, the EC’s System monitors HPAI cases in “captive birds” in a separate category. To date in 2026, 15 countries have notified the System of 123 outbreaks involving captive birds. During the whole of last year, 25 countries registered 175 outbreaks in this category with the EC. HPAI-related developments affecting Europe’s poultry sector Based on the changing HPAI situation in the region, Germany’s veterinary reference laboratory Friedrich-Loeffler Institute has raised the disease risk level for the nation’s poultry flocks. The risk is now seen as “moderate” for both the transmission of H5 viruses to poultry and captive birds directly or indirectly from the wild population, and between wild birds within the country. Last month, EU member states agreed with a proposal from the European Commission Directorate for Agriculture, DG Agriculture and Rural Development (DG-AGRI) to release funds from the agricultural reserve to compensate Italian farmers hit by previous HPAI outbreaks. EUR61 million (US$68 million) will be directed to poultry and egg farmers whose businesses were impacted by measures taken to control and prevent the spread of infection between September of 2022 and March of 2025. Payments must be made to the recipients by May of next year. More widespread HPAI cases in wild birds As of October 7, a total of 2,709 HPAI outbreaks in Europe’s wild population had been logged by the EC’s System by 33 countries in 2026. Of these, the H5N1 virus serotype was involved in around 2,660, while the rest were identified as belonging to the H5 group. Based on EC data, wild birds infected with the H5N1 variant have been recorded by Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden over the past month. Following a hiatus of around 18 months, the same virus was detected again on the Mediterranean island of Cyprus in September, according to a recent WOAH notification. The same agency has been notified about the first wild birds that have tested positive for H5N1 since the start of the HPAI “season.” Six birds were found dead at four locations in England. Over the past month, WOAH has been informed about seven wild birds in Iceland that have tested positive for the H5N5 virus serotype. Transcriptomic Study Showing Limited Host-Species Effect 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年10月15日 来源:Viruses 3.5 编辑推荐: 在第41次中国南极考察(2024–2025)期间,研究人员从Ardley岛同域分布的Adélie企鹅、帽带企鹅(chinstrap penguins)和巴布亚企鹅(gentoo penguins)采集新鲜粪便样本。通过转录组测序(transcriptomic 欢迎领取《类器官应用方案 3D之旅》 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 Article Open access 在第41次中国南极考察(2024–2025)期间,研究人员从Ardley岛同域分布的Adélie企鹅、帽带企鹅(chinstrap penguins)和巴布亚企鹅(gentoo penguins)采集新鲜粪便样本。通过转录组测序(transcriptomic sequencing)结合病毒contig组装,系统分析了粪便病毒组(faecal viromes)。共注释到32个已知病毒科(viral families),但超过一半的病毒reads仍未分类,表明南极企鹅肠道中存在大量未表征的病毒多样性(uncharacterised viral diversity)。未检测到病毒丰度或α多样性(alpha-diversity)的显著种间差异,宿主物种(host-species)对病毒群落结构仅产生微弱影响。虽然未检测到H5N1高致病性禽流感(H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza)和新城疫病毒(Newcastle disease virus),但回收了若干潜在病原体,包括δ冠状病毒(deltacoronaviruses)、新型星状病毒(novel astroviruses)和小RNA病毒(picornaviruses)。该工作为南极Pygoscelis企鹅建立了基线病毒组数据,并为极地野生动物长期病原监测和病毒溢出风险(viral spillover risk)评估提供了有价值见解。 论文主体部分解读 瑞孚迪自动化解决方案>>领 取 研究背景方面,Ardley岛位于南极半岛西部Fildes Peninsula区域,毗邻南设得兰群岛的King George Island,是海洋性南极最大无冰区之一。与南极大陆相比,该岛相对温和的温度和较多降水维持了多样筑巢海鸟种群和广泛植被。三种同域Pygoscelis企鹅,即Adélie、gentoo和chinstrap企鹅,在该岛繁殖。长期宿主–病毒共进化使这些企鹅维持低致病性病毒的稳定储库,包括禽流感病毒、星状病毒(astroviruses)、副黏病毒(paramyxoviruses)、圆环病毒(circoviruses)、腺病毒(adenoviruses)和多瘤病毒(polyomaviruses)。尽管病毒检测报告不断增加,但同域物种间病毒组组成和种间病毒多样性的系统比较仍然缺乏,这受限于样本量小和病毒覆盖不完整。为填补该知识空白,研究人员在2024年12月至2025年4月采集三种Pygoscelis企鹅新鲜粪便样本,利用转录组测序、病毒contig组装和分类注释,表征病毒群落、种间病毒多样性以及高风险病原分布,从而为极地生态系统长期野生动物监测和生态风险评估建立基线病毒组数据集。 研究人员开展的研究表明,共获得32个合格粪便转录组样本,其中14份来自Adélie企鹅、9份来自chinstrap企鹅、9份来自gentoo企鹅。研究共注释到32个已知病毒科,超过一半病毒reads未分类。病毒丰度和α多样性无显著种间差异,宿主物种对病毒群落结构仅呈弱效应。所有样本均未检测到H5N1 HPAIV或新城疫病毒(Newcastle disease virus, NDV)。同时,研究人员回收了若干潜在病原体,包括δ冠状病毒(deltacoronaviruses)、新型星状病毒(novel astroviruses)和小RNA病毒(picornaviruses)。该研究为南极Pygoscelis企鹅建立基线病毒组数据,并为极地野生动物长期病原监测和病毒溢出风险(viral spillover risk)评估提供重要依据。 为开展研究,关键技术方法如下:样本队列来源为2024年12月至2025年4月在Ardley岛采集的Adélie、chinstrap和gentoo企鹅新鲜粪便,样本以RNAlater保存于?80 °C;宿主物种通过形态特征和线粒体COI基因序列比对确认。提取总RNA后建库,并在DNBSEQ-T7平台进行PE 150 bp测序。使用FastQC和Trimmomatic质控,MEGAHIT进行从头组装,DIAMOND-BLASTX和BLASTN搜索NCBI nr/nt数据库,E值设为10?10,Bowtie2、SAMtools和CoverM定量TPM。多样性分析采用Kruskal–Wallis检验、Bray–Curtis距离、PERMANOVA、NMDS、PCoA和Ward聚类;系统发育分析采用MAFFT、IQ-TREE最大似然法(ML)1000次bootstrap、FigTree和pheatmap。 研究结果如下。 3.1 样本采集与宿主物种组成(Sample Collection and Host Species Composition):样本采集于Ardley岛邻近中国长城站的区域,时间为2024年12月至2025年2月。研究人员对chinstrap、Adélie和gentoo企鹅新鲜粪便进行总核酸提取、文库制备和转录组测序,共获得32个合格粪便转录组样本。结合野外形态观察和线粒体COI基因序列比对确认宿主物种,样本包括14份Adélie企鹅、9份chinstrap企鹅和9份gentoo企鹅。 3.2 粪便样本病毒群落组成与多样性(Composition and Diversity of Viral Communities in Faecal Samples):32个粪便转录组文库完成测序,质控后各样本clean reads为38.33百万至75.50百万,平均54.77百万,测序深度足以进行病毒组表征。研究共识别32个已知病毒科;去除噬菌体和逆转录病毒后,保留23个已知真核病毒种用于下游分析。未分类序列占三种宿主所有病毒reads的一半以上,表明南极企鹅肠道生态系统存在大量未描述病毒多样性。注释病毒包括RNA和DNA病毒群。主要RNA病毒类群包括Picornaviridae、Coronaviridae、Astroviridae、Paramyxoviridae和Rountreeviridae;Picornaviridae在chinstrap和Adélie企鹅中较gentoo企鹅更丰富,Coronaviridae在Adélie企鹅中高度富集;藻类和植物来源RNA病毒也被检测到,被认为来自企鹅饮食摄入。主要DNA病毒包括Herpesviridae、Adenoviridae和Poxviridae,以及巨型DNA病毒(Pandoraviridae、Mimiviridae、Schizomimiviridae);Herpesviridae在chinstrap企鹅中偏好积累,巨型DNA病毒在gentoo企鹅中丰度较高;藻类和植物DNA病毒(Phycodnaviridae、Caulimoviridae)也被鉴定为食源性污染物。所有粪便样本均未检测到H5N1 HPAIV或NDV。α多样性方面,基于物种丰富度和Shannon指数的Kruskal–Wallis检验显示,三种企鹅间病毒物种丰富度(p = 0.085)和Shannon多样性(p = 0.294)无显著差异。β多样性方面,基于Bray–Curtis距离的PCoA前两轴累计解释29.5%总变异(PCoA1为18.5%,PCoA2为11.1%),NMDS结果一致(Stress = 0.227);PERMANOVA检测到宿主物种对病毒群落结构有统计学显著影响(R2 = 0.097,p = 0.021),但低R2值表明宿主过滤作用弱,宿主物种不驱动形成物种特异性病毒组。多数样本间组成差异来自宿主个体特征、饮食差异、环境暴露和随机过程。 3.3 Adélie企鹅来源δ冠状病毒基因组与系统发育特征(Genomic and Phylogenetic Characteristics of Adélie Penguin-Derived Deltacoronavirus):研究人员从单个Adélie企鹅粪便样本1227-13成功组装近完整δ冠状病毒基因组,长度为26,196 nt。该病毒被正式命名为“Adélie penguin deltacoronavirus”。基于trimmed基因组序列和RNA依赖的RNA聚合酶(RdRp)复制酶基因序列构建最大似然系统发育树,结果显示该株属于Coronaviridae的Buldecovirus亚属,并与2023年从南极鞘嘴鸟中回收的δ冠状病毒以及2014年最初在gentoo企鹅中鉴定的δ冠状病毒序列聚类。基因组比较显示,该分离株与2023年南极鞘嘴鸟δ冠状病毒(GenBank accession: PQ351810.1)核苷酸同一性最高,为96.23%。基于RdRp的系统发育分析表明,极地δ冠状病毒分离株与其它大陆禽类群体中流行的δ冠状病毒存在显著遗传分化。这些发现提示δ冠状病毒在南极海鸟间持续跨种传播,并出现独特的南极δ冠状病毒谱系。 3.4 企鹅星状病毒基因组与系统发育特征(Genomic and Phylogenetic Characteristics of Penguin Astrovirus):研究人员回收了近全长星状病毒基因组,编码ORF1a、ORF1b(RdRp)和ORF2衣壳蛋白。基于RdRp和衣壳蛋白氨基酸序列分别构建系统发育树,并辅以序列同一性热图分析。系统发育分析将该分离株置于Avastrovirus属,正式命名为“Penguin astrovirus 2025”。先前报道的南极星状病毒在树上分散,未能形成单一单系极地进化枝。同源分析显示,该企鹅分离株的RdRp和ORF2序列与来自其它大陆的代表性星状病毒株相比,序列同一性显著低于公认星状病毒种界定阈值(RdRp核苷酸为83%,衣壳蛋白为75%)。因此,该分离株被提议代表一个新的星状病毒种。 3.5 企鹅Picornaviridae和Caliciviridae基因组与系统发育特征(Genomic and Phylogenetic Characteristics of Penguin Picornaviridae and Caliciviridae):除Coronaviridae和Astroviridae外,病毒组分析显示Picornaviridae和Caliciviridae是企鹅粪便样本中丰富的病毒组分,并组装到多个归属这两个科的病毒contig。基于推导的RdRp氨基酸序列分别构建Picornaviridae和Caliciviridae最大似然系统发育树。Picornaviridae序列分散于该科多个属,包括Hepatovirus、Megrivirus及若干未分类picorna-like viruses,反映高谱系多样性;其中若干病毒进化枝与禽、海洋哺乳动物和蝙蝠宿主来源病毒近缘。四个Caliciviridae序列聚类在Goosecalicivirus进化枝内,并形成两个明显亚簇,与鹅来源禽类calicivirus系统发育关系最近,且与Caliciviridae内其它属明显分离。主要分支获得稳健节点bootstrap支持。 讨论部分总结:该研究系统表征了三种同域南极企鹅的粪便病毒组,识别32个已知病毒科,其中超过一半序列仍未分类。该高比例未分类序列表明南极企鹅肠道生态系统是丰富且仍大量未描述病毒多样性的储库。公共病毒参考数据库不完整,加上短读长转录组数据,限制了许多新型病毒contig的准确分类注释。病毒丰度和α多样性在物种间无显著差异。β多样性分析表明宿主物种显著影响病毒群落组成,但低决定系数提示宿主物种密度对病毒群落结构贡献有限。病毒群落大多数变异来自个体特征、饮食变异、环境暴露和随机生态过程。饮食来源的藻类和植物相关病毒频繁回收,进一步说明食物资源对肠道病毒组谱的影响。虽然未检测到H5N1或NDV等高致病性病毒,但鉴于采样范围和样本量受限,不能完全排除感染可能性。南极企鹅粪便病毒组中多个病毒科,包括Picornaviridae、Coronaviridae、Astroviridae和Caliciviridae,与温带家禽和其它禽类宿主常见肠道病毒群重叠。这支持一套核心病毒科在Aves中跨地理远距离区域广泛传播的观点。然而,许多南极病毒contig与温带禽类对应序列存在显著序列分化,提示病毒定殖南极生态系统后发生局部适应进化。与先前发现一致,Picornaviridae和Astroviridae构成企鹅粪便样本中主要RNA病毒组分。值得注意的是,本研究表征的δ冠状病毒是首个从Adélie企鹅获得的近完整δ冠状病毒基因组。系统发育分析确认该病毒聚类于先前鉴定的南极海鸟δ冠状病毒谱系,支持δ冠状病毒可能在同域南极海鸟间经历反复跨种传播事件的假设。对于本研究表征的新型星状病毒,基于RdRp和衣壳蛋白的系统发育构建显示南极星状病毒呈多系分布。具体而言,Penguin astrovirus 2025聚类于禽类家禽和水禽相关的Avastrovirus Clade 1,而先前报道的Adélie企鹅星状病毒(KM587711)属于一个不同系统发育进化枝。该模式提示星状病毒谱系多次独立引入南极企鹅种群,而非单一古老极地地方性星状病毒祖先。同源重组是塑造Astroviridae成员遗传多样性的已确立进化力量。鉴于本研究数据集范围,未进行专门重组检测分析。这是本研究在物种界定和进化推断方面的关键限制。不过,分类归属得到两个独立遗传标记(RdRp和衣壳蛋白)支持,部分缓解了重组事件可能带来的系统发育混杂信号。尽管检测到的病毒主要引起无症状潜伏感染且当前无疫情暴发,其溢出风险仍不可忽视。外来病原的引入可驱动适应性突变、毒力增强和跨种传播。此外,高密度繁殖群和候鸟活动可能加速病毒在南极野生动物间的传播,可能破坏极地生态系统。因此,建立长期系统性病原监测对于追踪病毒动态和保障极地生态安全至关重要。 The project is supported by the Defense Threat Reduction Agency’s Joint Science and Technology Office (JSTO) through the Medical CBRN Defense Consortium. The agreement has a total estimated project cost of approximately $20.7 million over its period of performance, with funding provided incrementally. VITAL was selected under Reimagining Available Vaccines and Envisioning Novelty (RAVEN), a JSTO program focused on advancing multivalent prophylactic biological countermeasures. RAVEN seeks both improvements to existing technologies and new vaccine or preventive platforms capable of addressing multiple biological threats, moving beyond approaches that are focused on one threat at a time. The initial proof of concept will focus on a highly pathogenic avian influenza A virus, H5N1. ​​Researchers will develop an unmodified mRNA-based vaccine prototype designed for intranasal delivery that will restrict primarily the immunogen expression to immune cells known as macrophages in the respiratory tract, avoiding potential adverse events by expression of the antigen in other type of cells that do not participate in this process during natural infection. The program will evaluate how this targeting affects antigen presentation, immune stimulation, safety, and protection. “VITAL is designed to directly support RAVEN’s objective by asking a broader question than whether we can make a vaccine against one virus,” said Gustavo Palacios, PhD, Professor of Microbiology at the Icahn School of Medicine and VITAL project lead. “Rather than focusing only on which antigens are delivered, we want to understand which biological principles can be incorporated into vaccination so that the same framework can eventually be adapted across different respiratory threats. H5N1 gives us a rigorous starting point to test those principles.” The approach is built around five biological principles: ​​targeting exclusively the expression of the immunogen in immune cells that help activate the body’s immune response; providing appropriate stimulation to those cells; engineering antigens to reduce toxicity and adverse responses; matching antigen delivery to a pathogen’s natural route of entry; and ​​developing pulse immunization, a strategy designed to ​generate an immune response that ​mimic aspects of natural infection through controlled patterns of exposure. The program brings together complementary expertise in viral genomics, molecular virology, vaccine development, and human immunology from internationally renowned investigators, including Dr. Palacios, Adolfo García-Sastre, PhD, and Ana Fernandez-Sesma, PhD, all faculty members in the Department of Microbiology at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. A central component of VITAL is antigen detoxification: engineering viral antigens to reduce potential toxicity while preserving antigen expression and immunogenicity. The program will also investigate different intranasal immunization schedules, including repeated low-dose regimens designed to mimic aspects of the timing of natural infection. For Dr. García-Sastre, whose research has focused extensively on influenza virus biology, virus-host interactions, and vaccine development, VITAL provides an opportunity to explore new strategies for a longstanding challenge in influenza vaccination: generating long-lasting immune protection against a range of virus variants. “One of the central challenges in influenza vaccination is achieving protection that is broad and durable rather than narrowly focused on a single circulating influenza virus variant,” said Dr. García-Sastre, Irene and Dr. Arthur M. Fishberg Professor of Medicine and Director of the Global Health and Emerging Pathogens Institute at the Icahn School of Medicine. “VITAL gives us an opportunity to explore a different way of approaching that problem—by engineering not only the antigen, but also how, where, and over what time course the immune system encounters it.” To understand those responses in greater depth, VITAL will combine human immune tissue models and animal models with single-cell and spatial analysis, proteomics, and artificial intelligence and computational approaches. The research will examine how targeted antigen-presenting cells, such as macrophages and dendritic cells, respond to vaccination, interact with each other, and how those interactions contribute to downstream B and T cell responses. That component of the program aligns closely with Dr. Fernandez-Sesma’s research on virus-host interactions and immune responses in human systems, including work involving macrophages, dendritic cells, and human tonsil-based models. “A major strength of VITAL is the ability to study how vaccination shapes the immune response in physiologically relevant human systems,” said Dr. Fernandez-Sesma, Chair of the Department of Microbiology at the Icahn School of Medicine. “By looking closely at macrophages, dendritic cells, and other immune populations using primary human tissues, we can predict whether a vaccine generates the appropriate immune response in humans as an alternative to animal models.” If the initial principles are successfully validated, VITAL is structured to expand beyond H5N1. The program is designed to scale toward a multivalent strategy encompassing at least 20 respiratory viruses, creating a framework that can be evaluated across a broader range of respiratory threats. Preclinical studies will evaluate the durability and breadth of immune responses across multiple experimental systems, including young and aged mice and ferrets, in addition to the human primary systems mentioned above. Animal models remain necessary under the current regulatory framework to characterize integrated immune responses, safety, and protection in vivo. These studies provide a bridge to a future framework in which validated human organoid systems may be accepted by regulatory agencies for defined aspects of preclinical evaluation. ​​The program also includes regulatory planning and Investigational New Drug-enabling activities to support the potential clinical translation of selected vaccine candidates. The VITAL project agreement runs through August 28, 2031. Its comprehensive system includes seven hospitals, more than 400 outpatient practices, over 600 research and clinical laboratories, the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, the Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences, and the Mount Sinai Phillips School of Nursing. Together, the Health System comprises approximately 48,000 employees, more than 9,000 physicians, and 8,600 nurses. As a leading learning health system, Mount Sinai combines clinical expertise with scientific discovery to improve patient care while training the next generation of health care and biomedical leaders. The Health System provides care across every stage of life, from prenatal care through geriatrics, while advancing personalized medicine through artificial intelligence, data science, and biomedical research. Mount Sinai is consistently recognized among the nation’s leading academic health systems for patient care, research, and education. The Mount Sinai Hospital is ranked No. 1 in New York by Newsweek and No. 5 on the magazine’s World’s Best Hospitals list. The Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai ranks No. 11 among U.S. medical schools and No. 1 among freestanding medical schools for National Institutes of Health funding, reflecting the strength of its scientific enterprise and leadership in biomedical research. records.content: Breaking News Drones Hit Two Chemical Tankers in Black Sea, Eight Crew Members Missing Cityscape Bahrain Returns for Fifth Edition, Showcasing Real Estate Opportunities Huawei Showcases Intelligent Finance Innovation at Fintech Forward 2026 Bahrain Bourse Approves Abu Dhabi Islamic Securities as External Broker GFH Closes $63 Million Power Systems Opportunities Fund Drones Hit Two Chemical Tankers in Black Sea, Eight Crew Members Missing Cityscape Bahrain Returns for Fifth Edition, Showcasing Real Estate Opportunities Huawei Showcases Intelligent Finance Innovation at Fintech Forward 2026 Bahrain Bourse Approves Abu Dhabi Islamic Securities as External Broker GFH Closes $63 Million Power Systems Opportunities Fund Friday, 16 October 2026 عربيePaper News Views Videos ClassifiedsCampusCommunity More News Views Videos ClassifiedsCampusCommunity More SearchCtrl K Friday, 16 October 2026 Oct. 16 NewsViewsVideosClassifiedsCampusCommunity More NewsViewsVideosClassifiedsCampusCommunityMore Home News World 15 October 20265 min read Avian Cholera Blamed for Mass Penguin Deaths in Antarctica Scientists have identified avian cholera as the main cause of thousands of Adélie penguin deaths in 2024, revealing an overlooked disease threat in Antarctica amid concerns over bird flu. Sadiq Mohsen Published 15 October 2026, 12:17 Link copiedShare Save Thousands of Adélie penguins live in Antarctica’s remote Danger Islands. Thousands of Adélie penguins and other seabirds were found dead in Antarctica’s remote Danger Islands in March 2024. Laboratory tests detected the bacterium responsible for avian cholera in 46 of 49 sampled animals. Researchers say the findings highlight the need to monitor multiple diseases affecting Antarctic wildlife, not only bird flu. Thousands of penguins found dead in Antarctica in 2024 were primarily victims of avian cholera rather than bird flu, according to a new study that has revealed an overlooked threat to wildlife in the remote region. In Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences, examined a mass mortality event involving Adélie penguins and other seabirds in the Danger Islands archipelago off the Antarctic Peninsula. The discovery surprised researchers who initially suspected highly pathogenic avian influenza, commonly known as H5N1 bird flu, because the virus had recently reached Antarctica and raised concerns about its impact on local wildlife. However, laboratory testing and examinations of the animals revealed that avian cholera was responsible for most of the investigated deaths. Thousands of penguins found dead Dead penguins discovered during the expedition. In March 2024, an international research expedition visited the Danger Islands, which are home to more than 1.2 million breeding pairs of Adélie penguins. Researchers encountered thousands of dead penguins across two islands, alongside carcasses belonging to other seabird species. The scale of the deaths prompted concerns about a possible outbreak of bird flu. The H5N1 virus had recently spread to Antarctica, and scientists were investigating whether it was responsible for the sudden loss of wildlife. Researchers collected samples from 49 carcasses for laboratory analysis. The results showed that DNA from Pasteurella multocida, the bacterium that causes avian cholera, was detected in 46 of the sampled animals. H5N1 was detected in only a few. The findings identified avian cholera as the cause of most of the deaths investigated, demonstrating the importance of considering other diseases even when a major known pathogen is circulating. What is avian cholera? Scientists investigate the cause of death. Avian cholera is a contagious bacterial disease that affects birds and can cause severe illness and sudden death. It is caused by Pasteurella multocida, a bacterium that can spread through contact with infected animals and contaminated environments. In dense breeding colonies, where large numbers of birds gather, outbreaks can have serious consequences. Despite its name, avian cholera is different from the cholera that affects humans. The disease can progress rapidly, with bacteria spreading through the bloodstream and affecting multiple organs. This can make outbreaks particularly damaging when many birds are living in close proximity. Researchers say the latest findings show that avian cholera deserves greater attention in studies of Antarctic wildlife mortality. A disease that may have circulated for decades Genetic analysis revealed that the bacterial strain involved in the outbreak was closely related to one identified in Antarctic seabirds more than two decades ago. The researchers also found genetic links with strains detected elsewhere in the Southern Ocean, including locations thousands of kilometers away. These similarities suggest that the disease may be more widely distributed in the region than previously recognised. The findings do not establish a continuous record of outbreaks over the entire period, but they provide evidence that avian cholera has been present in the wider Antarctic environment for many years. Lead author Matteo Iervolino and his colleagues highlighted the importance of continued wildlife-health surveillance, particularly in remote locations where disease outbreaks can go undetected or remain unexplained. Why bird flu was initially suspected The discovery of H5N1 in Antarctica had raised concerns among scientists about the vulnerability of seabirds and marine mammals to the virus. Because bird flu can cause substantial mortality in wildlife, researchers initially considered it a likely explanation for the penguin deaths. However, the new study demonstrates that the presence of one concerning pathogen does not mean it is responsible for every mass mortality event. Researchers stressed that a broad investigation of infectious diseases is necessary to determine what is killing wildlife, especially when several pathogens may be circulating in the same region. The study does not suggest that bird flu is harmless to Antarctic animals. Instead, it shows that other diseases can cause significant losses and should not be overlooked. Protecting Antarctica’s wildlife The findings underline the challenges of monitoring wildlife in one of the world’s most remote environments. Antarctica’s isolation makes it difficult to investigate animal deaths quickly, while large breeding colonies can make outbreaks particularly consequential. Researchers say sustained monitoring could help scientists identify the causes of future mortality events and better understand how infectious diseases affect seabirds. The latest research does not establish that avian cholera alone threatens the entire Adélie penguin population with extinction. However, it identifies the disease as an important cause of mortality that requires further investigation. For scientists, the discovery is a reminder that protecting Antarctic wildlife requires more than monitoring a single virus. Understanding the range of pathogens circulating in the region will be essential to assessing future risks to penguins and other seabirds. He regularly researches and writes news reports, interviews and human-interest stories, presenting complex developments in a clear and accessible newspaper style. His reporting also involves following breaking news, verifying information from multiple sources and developing timely story angles for print and digital audiences. BREAKINGREAD MORE Avian flu confirmed in multiple goose flocks in Reno-Sparks, agencies warn by Katherine Nowicki Wed, October 14, 2026 at 2:04 PM Updated Wed, October 14, 2026 at 2:09 PM FILE -This colorized electron microscope image released by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases on March 26, 2024, shows avian influenza A H5N1 virus particles (yellow), grown in Madin-Darby Canine Kidney (MDCK) epithelial cells (blue). (CDC/NIAID via AP, File) 1Comment Share topics: Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza Reno-Sparks Nevada Department of Wildlife Nevada Department of Agriculture Public health Wild geese Dead bird reporting HPAI symptoms The Nevada Department of Wildlife (NDOW) in coordination with the Nevada Department of Agriculture, and Nevada Division of Public and Behavioral Health confirmed an outbreak of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) in multiple flocks of geese in the Reno/Sparks region. Officials say the public can help by identifying infected geese, notifying the proper officials and disposing geese safely to reduce transmission to other birds and species. HPAI is a highly contagious virus that can infect poultry, wild waterfowl, and in rare cases can infect livestock and humans. HPAI symptoms in birds include: Sneezing, coughing, eye & nasal discharge, swelling or fluid accumulating around one or both eyes. Abnormal position of head or neck, poor balance and coordination, and/or circling. A buildup of fluid in the bird’s legs and patchy redness of the skin. Diarrhea and green discoloration of the feces. Weakness, lethargy, depression. Sudden death. If the public encounters a dead goose, officials encourage them to do the following: Powered By 10 Duane Davis sentenced 40 years to life in prison for murder of Tupac Shakur Share Next Stay Notify the landowner responsible. For geese found on City or County Parks, contact them for removal. City of Reno Parks can be reached at (775) 334-2270; Washoe County Parks phone is (775) 828-6612. Dispose waterfowl on your own property by double bagging it and placing it in municipal waste. Be sure to wear gloves, an N95 mask, and eye protection. If you encounter a dead goose and have poultry, please change your clothes and shoes afterwards. If the public encounters a sick goose, they are encouraged to: Leave the goose alone and contact NDOW at (775) 688-1500 to report the location of the goose. If this is on your property, someone will contact you as soon as possible. Keep pets and children away. If you have domestic birds, especially backyard poultry officials say you should do the following: Keep poultry in secure enclosures away from wild birds and waterfowl. Wear dedicated clothing and footwear when caring for poultry. Clean and disinfect tools and equipment after use. Store poultry feed securely and avoid placing wild bird feeders near poultry areas. Watch for unusual behavior, signs of illness or unexpected deaths in your flock. Avoid touching or handling sick or dead wild birds. Use gloves and protective gear when necessary. Contact a veterinarian if birds appear sick and report high mortality rates among domestic poultry to the NDA at diseasereporting@agri.nv.gov. Officials say HPAI rarely spreads to livestock and humans. In wild waterfowl populations, it usually displays without any signs of illness and low mortality rates. It can cause mortality in some species of geese, raptors and game birds. Poultry are highly susceptible to HPAI and mortality rates may exceed 90%. When HPAI does spread to humans, symptoms may include fever, cough, sore throat, difficulty breathing, eye irritation, headaches, runny or stuffy nose, body aches, diarrhea and vomiting. Transmission to humans may occur from contact with infected or potentially infected animals, animal carcasses, or surfaces contaminated with animal excretions without using proper protective clothing and equipment. If you or your family have been exposed to a sick or dead bird and develop any of these symptoms, contact your healthcare provider and let them know about your animal exposure. Contact Economic Players EN FRANCAIS News Entrepreneurs LOGISTIC HUB Business environment Indicators Recent reforms Panorama Legal and administrative framework Sectors Agriculture Energy Finance - Banking Mining Training Telecom News Entrepreneurs LOGISTIC HUB Business environment Indicators Recent reforms Panorama Legal and administrative framework Sectors Agriculture Energy Finance - Banking Mining Training Telecom Seven West African Countries Adopt Three Regional Animal Health Strategies Agriculture Wednesday, 14 October 2026 15:29 (Togo First) - Ministers overseeing the livestock sector in seven West African countries adopted three regional strategies to combat transboundary animal diseases at an October 8 meeting in Lomé, Togo. The action plans run from 2026 to 2031 and focus on protecting donkeys, preventing foot-and-mouth disease and controlling highly pathogenic avian influenza. Improving Regional Coordination Developed by the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) Regional Animal Health Center (RAHC), the strategies aim to align national policies, strengthen disease surveillance and improve animal health data sharing. The measures include putting information systems into operation, aligning national regulations and improving coordination among disease surveillance networks. The goal is to detect outbreaks earlier and coordinate responses across countries, in line with the One Health approach, which addresses health risks affecting people, animals and the environment. Economic Impact of Animal Diseases Animal diseases also pose economic risks across the region, where livestock production supports rural livelihoods and food security. According to figures published by Togo First, the livestock subsector accounted for nearly 7% of Togo's GDP and more than 16% of agricultural GDP, with agriculture itself contributing about 40% of the country's GDP. Disease outbreaks can also disrupt livestock production. In March 2025, Togo reported H5N1 bird flu cases at three farms, affecting nearly 6,500 birds. Authorities responded by culling affected birds and restricting poultry movements. At the Lomé meeting, ministers also emphasized the need to strengthen vaccination programs, tighten controls on animal movements and increase participation by livestock farmers' organizations. In Togo, the measures are consistent with broader efforts to increase livestock productivity and make the sector more resilient. ENFORCING CONTRACTS (more info) Compared to some years ago when it was one of the lowest rankers under the Doing Business’ Enforcing Contracts indicator, Togo, leveraging many efforts to improve its business climate, was able to jump significantly on the index in the recent years... . CONTRACT EXECUTION (more info) Creation of special chambers of commerce for small debts • Creation of chambers of commerce at the Court of Appeal • Civil and commercial cases now handled by distinct clerks • Establishment of commercial courts in Lomé and Kara • Lawyers and bailiffs now have access to the FORSETI COMMERCIAL platform • A maximum period of 100 days was fixed to settle a commercial dispute . TRADING ACROSS BORDERS (more info) In comparison to previous years,Togo has significantly improved its ranking under the“Trading across borders” indicator by adopting multiple reforms that focus mainly on the digitization and reduction in delays, for import and export procedures related to import and export. In comparison to previous years, Togo has significantly improved its ranking on the “Trading across borders” index by adopting multiple reforms that focus mainly on the digitalization and reduction in delays, for import and export procedures related to import and export. CONSTRUCTION PERMIT (more info) After moving from the 133rd to 127th place under the 2020 Doing Business’ construction permit index, Togo intends to reiterate this feat in the coming edition of the global ranking. To this end, it has introduced this year multiple reforms. GETTING ELECTRICITY (more info) Over the past two years, Togo’s ranking under the Doing Business’ Getting electricity and water indicator has increased consistently. Owing this performance to multiple reforms aimed at making it easier for businesses to access power and water, Lomé plans to introduce even more reforms this year to keep up its improvements. REGISTERING A PROPERTY (more info) Out of all the 'Doing Business’ indicators, Property Registration is where Togo has improved the most since 2018. Indeed, after spending years in the lowest part of this ranking, the country now seeks to beat Rwanda which is the best performer on this index in Africa. To do so, Lomé has been introducing many reforms, with the latest batch implemented this year. PUBLIC PROCUREMENT (more info) From professionalization to digitization, through legislative regulations, Togo’s public procurement framework is constantly being modernized. Several reforms have been implemented to improve the sector much to the benefit of the private sector, which is the focus of the National Development Plan. PAYING TAXES AND DUTIES (more info) To improve its business environment, Togo introduced some important reforms related to the payment of tax and duties. From the replacement of some taxes to the cancellation of others through exemptions, the country has only one objective: offer the most attractive tax framework to investors and economic operators. Officials say the public can help by identifying infected geese, notifying the proper officials and disposing geese safely to reduce transmission to other birds and species. HPAI is a highly contagious virus that can infect poultry, wild waterfowl, and in rare cases can infect livestock and humans. HPAI symptoms in birds include: Sneezing, coughing, eye & nasal discharge, swelling or fluid accumulating around one or both eyes. Abnormal position of head or neck, poor balance and coordination, and/or circling. A buildup of fluid in the bird’s legs and patchy redness of the skin. Diarrhea and green discoloration of the feces. Weakness, lethargy, depression. Sudden death. If the public encounters a dead goose, officials encourage them to do the following: Notify the landowner responsible. For geese found on City or County Parks, contact them for removal. City of Reno Parks can be reached at (775) 334-2270; Washoe County Parks phone is (775) 828-6612. Dispose waterfowl on your own property by double bagging it and placing it in municipal waste. Be sure to wear gloves, an N95 mask, and eye protection. If you encounter a dead goose and have poultry, please change your clothes and shoes afterwards. If the public encounters a sick goose, they are encouraged to: Leave the goose alone and contact NDOW at (775) 688-1500 to report the location of the goose. If this is on your property, someone will contact you as soon as possible. Keep pets and children away. If you have domestic birds, especially backyard poultry officials say you should do the following: Keep poultry in secure enclosures away from wild birds and waterfowl. Wear dedicated clothing and footwear when caring for poultry. Clean and disinfect tools and equipment after use. Store poultry feed securely and avoid placing wild bird feeders near poultry areas. Watch for unusual behavior, signs of illness or unexpected deaths in your flock. Avoid touching or handling sick or dead wild birds. Use gloves and protective gear when necessary. Contact a veterinarian if birds appear sick and report high mortality rates among domestic poultry to the NDA at diseasereporting@agri.nv.gov. Officials say HPAI rarely spreads to livestock and humans. In wild waterfowl populations, it usually displays without any signs of illness and low mortality rates. It can cause mortality in some species of geese, raptors and game birds. Poultry are highly susceptible to HPAI and mortality rates may exceed 90%. When HPAI does spread to humans, symptoms may include fever, cough, sore throat, difficulty breathing, eye irritation, headaches, runny or stuffy nose, body aches, diarrhea and vomiting. Transmission to humans may occur from contact with infected or potentially infected animals, animal carcasses, or surfaces contaminated with animal excretions without using proper protective clothing and equipment. If you or your family have been exposed to a sick or dead bird and develop any of these symptoms, contact your healthcare provider and let them know about your animal exposure. It is increasingly a practical framework for protecting profitability, reducing resource losses and securing the future of animal protein production. ADM’s approach aligns with its Next Generation Thinking strategy, which focuses on helping customers improve resource efficiency, production performance, and environmental outcomes. For animal nutrition professionals, sustainability can be viewed through 3 connected pillars: economic, environmental and social sustainability. Economic sustainability is the foundation of resilient production systems. A farm, integrator or feed business must remain profitable to continue investing in better practices, new technologies and long-term improvement. Feed cost efficiency, lower mortality, fewer downgraded products, improved feed conversion and longer productive lifespans all contribute directly to that objective. Environmental sustainability focuses on producing animal protein while using fewer natural resources and reducing pressure on land, water, air and biodiversity. In feed, this means improving nutrient efficiency, reducing nitrogen, phosphorus and mineral excretion, limiting avoidable waste and responsible sourcing raw materials. ADM supports these efforts through traceability and responsible sourcing programs aligned with its ambition to develop deforestation – and conversion – free supply chains, particularly in areas identified as having a greater risk of deforestation and ecosystem conversion. Social sustainability completes the picture by supporting safe, transparent and responsible food systems. It includes animal welfare, food safety, responsible use of resources, and the long-term viability of the people, farms and communities involved across the agricultural value chain. Starting with economics: The SINCRO treasure hunt ADM’s SINCRO service offering is based on a clear principle: progress must be measurable. The journey therefore begins with economic sustainability. By analysing technical and economic results, SINCRO helps identify where value is being lost and where growth opportunities can be captured. This is especially relevant in an industry where small performance gaps can translate into significant financial impact at farm or feed mill level. This approach can be compared to a treasure hunt. In many production systems, hidden losses are present in the data: a slightly higher feed conversion ratio, marginally increased mortality, downgraded eggs, reduced animal longevity, or inconsistent raw material quality. Individually, these gaps may appear limited. When converted into economic value, however, they can reveal substantial sources of lost profit. ADM illustrates this logic through digital tools such as TreasurePerform, which helps convert technical gaps versus a reference into economic losses. A difference in feed conversion ratio, mortality, laying persistency or egg discard rate can be expressed in monetary terms, making priorities easier to discuss and decisions easier to make. This first diagnostic step creates the basis for targeted actions, combining services, expertise and solutions to improve technical performance and strengthen economic sustainability. From grain to farm: A holistic route to environmental sustainability Raw material sourcing has a major influence on the carbon footprint of animal feed. Using verified deforestation-free raw materials can reduce deforestation-related supply chain risk and may lower certain environmental impacts associated with feed ingredient sourcing, depending on the sourcing scenario and assessment methodology. ADM supports customers with traceable sourcing solutions and responsible supply chain programs designed to reduce risks linked to deforestation and conversion. Its soy strategy included traceability, supplier engagement, risk assessment and monitoring aimed at reducing deforestation and land-conversion risks within high-risk sourcing regions. As customers increasingly seek to quantify the environmental impact of feed ingredients, access to credible life cycle assessment (LCA) data has become an important component of responsible sourcing. ADM offers products supported by Global Feed LCA Institute (GFLI)-branded life cycle assessment data, including soybean meal and palm kernel expeller, enabling customers to make more informed sourcing decisions and support transparent environmental reporting. For palm kernel expeller, this verified data demonstrates up to a 25% lower carbon footprint compared with conventional alternatives, illustrating how ingredient selection can contribute to measurable emissions reductions across both the feed supply chain and livestock production. Precision nutrition is another practical lever for improving sustainability. It helps nutritionists formulate closer to animals’ real requirements while limiting excess nutrients and avoidable waste. This starts with accurate characterization of raw materials, including their quality and variability. Through SINCRO, ADM helps customers access laboratory analyses and NIR calibrations to support their quality control programs. ADM’s MatrixNutri app supports this approach by converting analytical results for more than 400 ingredients into precise, species-specific nutritional values, including values for aquaculture and providing a robust foundation for accurate feed formulation. Together, these services are designed to help reduce resource losses associated with formulation variability while supporting profitability thereby supporting both environmental and economic goals. A practical example can be seen in a broiler trial conducted by ADM in which crude protein in the finisher diet was reduced from 19% to 16.2% in parallel to specific adjustments. Final live weight was maintained, while total protein intake decreased. In this trial, modelling indicated that the carbon footprint of the finisher feed was up to 17% lower than the reference formulation. At farm gate, modelling indicated lower environmental impacts per kg of meat produced for the indicators assessed in the study. This illustrates how ADM’s nutrition expertise can help customers move beyond least-cost formulation toward a broader optimization model that integrates economic, zootechnical, and environmental objectives. ADM’s broad portfolio of feed additives and specialty solutions complements its grain-to-farm approach by helping customers reduce production losses and improve resource efficiency and farm performance. Improving eggshell quality, for example, can reduce the number of downgraded or discarded eggs. Supporting laying hen longevity can reduce the non-productive investment represented by replacement pullets. Improving sow robustness and reproductive performance can reduce culling and save resources. Organic trace mineral solutions, such as the B-Traxim range, can support mineralbioavailability, thereby contributing to lower mineral excretion. In this context, ADM’s Next Generation Thinking strategy is not positioned as an opposition between profitability and sustainability. Rather, it shows that both objectives can reinforce each other when data, nutrition expertise and field performance are connected. By reducing technical gaps, improving nutrient use and animal robustness, limiting waste and supporting responsible raw materials sourcing, animal feed professionals can create more efficient production systems that are economically robust and designed to use resources more efficiently and reduce production losses. Conclusion: Building sustainable value through measurable improvement For the animal feed industry, the most effective sustainability strategies are those that can be measured, implemented and translated into value. ADM’s approach starts with economic performance because profitability gives producers the capacity to invest, adapt and improve. From there, SINCRO connects control of raw materials, precision nutrition and performance monitoring to help reduce variability and unlock hidden opportunities. ADM feed additives and specialty solutions provide another practical lever, helping improve nutrient efficiency, animal robustness, product quality and loss reduction across species and production systems. Actions that improve farm profitability, such as better feed efficiency, fewer losses, stronger animal robustness, longer productive lifespans and more accurate formulation, can also lower the use of natural resources. Responsible sourcing and traceability help address environmental risks associated with key raw materials, including land-use change and deforestation, before those materials enter the feed mill. This holistic model shows that sustainability is not a separate agenda for animal nutrition, but an integrated process supported by ADM at each step of the value chain. By combining sourcing expertise, analytical tools, nutrition services, performance monitoring and tailored solutions, ADM can help customers build more competitive, transparent and resilient production systems for the future.Learn more about ADM’s SINCRO solutions here. Wildlife Biologists Start Vaccinating Shy Albatrosses by Hand, Taking Aim at the Spread of Avian Flu in Tasmania If all goes to plan, officials hope to vaccinate up to 100 of the large seabirds on Albatross Island, giving each two doses of the vaccine. Afterward, they plan to keep tabs on the birds using remote cameras and follow-up visits Sarah Kuta | Daily Correspondent October 15, 2026 11:21 a.m. Share Copy linkEmailSMSFacebookXRedditLinkedInBlueskyPrint Add as preferred source Biologists are running a pilot project with up to 100 birds on Albatross Island. Department of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania Wildlife officials in Australia are taking a hands-on approach to combating the deadly and highly contagious bird flu strain H5N1. Veterinarians and biologists have just begun a multi-week pilot project to capture and vaccinate shy albatrosses on a remote Tasmanian island. So far, the albatrosses have remained healthy and free from the virus. However, the avian flu recently reached Tasmania for the first time, and it has sickened dozens of birds from other species since then. Wildlife experts consider the shy albatross highly vulnerable to the H5N1 strain, so they’re taking steps to protect them. Officials hope the results of the pilot project will inform their broader efforts to combat the avian influenza “at a population level” in the species, Sheryl Hamilton, a wildlife biologist with Tasmania’s Department of Natural Resources and Environment, tells Kelsey Reid of the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC). Officials hope the pilot project will inform their broader approach to vaccinating the birds. Department of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania The shy albatross is a large seabird that breeds on three islets in the Bass Strait between the Australian mainland and the island state of Tasmania: Albatross Island, Mewstone and Pedra Branca. They’re considered “near threatened” by the International Union for Conservation of Nature and “vulnerable” in Tasmania. The total population includes an estimated 15,000 breeding pairs. If all goes to plan, officials hope to vaccinate up to 100 shy albatrosses on Albatross Island, giving each bird two doses of the vaccine. Afterward, they plan to keep an eye on the birds using remote cameras and follow-up visits to see how they respond. The process is labor-intensive. Wearing head-to-toe hazmat suits, wildlife biologists pick up each bird by hand, weigh it and administer the first dose of the vaccine. They then mark the birds with temporary, nontoxic paint and place numbered markers at their nests to keep track of which individuals are part of the project. They plan to return in a few weeks to administer the second dose. Vaccinating wild birds is difficult because they’re hard to catch and constantly on the move, making it challenging to recapture them for a second dose. However, shy albatrosses provide a “unique opportunity,” since they can be safely approached multiple times while nesting and monitored “in a way that’s not possible for many wild species,” Guy Barnett, the Tasmanian minister for environment and climate change, says in a statement. Veterinarians have also been vaccinating little penguins against the bird flu on Phillip Island and St Kilda beach in Victoria, Australia. The squat, black-and-white birds don’t fly, and they return to the same spot each night, making them relatively easy to catch for both doses. So far, more than 1,500 birds have received their first dose. Did you know? Airlifting nests In 2017, biologists airlifted artificial shy albatross nests to Albatross Island in a bid to boost the species’ breeding success. Warmer and wetter weather, driven by climate change, had been making it harder for the birds’ natural nests to stay together, biologists said. Tasmania recorded its first official case of the bird flu in August, when a brown skua found on the island’s northwest coast tested positive. Since then, the number of bird flu “events”—in which the virus is detected in one or more animals—has risen to 50, with a Pacific gull, a great crested tern, a little penguin and a black currawong among the latest species affected by the virus, reports Olivia Hicks for 7BU. The virus has not been detected in commercial poultry or backyard flocks, and Tasmania has not experienced any mass mortality events. Australia had been the only continent without avian influenza until June, when the virus was detected in wild seabirds in the state of Western Australia. Since then, the bird flu has sickened a variety of seabirds and mammals on the continent and its surrounding islands, from greater ‌crested terns to long-nosed fur seals. The virus has also been detected in endangered Australian sea lions and urban foxes. So far, the virus has not been detected in shy albatrosses. Department of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania Across Australia, officials have recorded 706 total bird flu events at last count. Officials are concerned about the spread of the virus in Australia and New Zealand, which are home to many vulnerable species found nowhere else on Earth. The situation is “quite frightening,” Rachael Gray, a veterinary pathologist at the University of Sydney, tells ABC’s Jacinta Bowler and Peter de Kruijff. “It’s pretty overwhelming at the moment,” she adds. “These animals, who we very much love and admire and respect ... these animals are getting sick, they are suffering and then they are dying.” You Might Also Like Birds in Their Pants: Two Men Accused of Smuggling 21 Avians After Miami Airport Bust October 15, 2026 Construction Work on the North Dakota Governor's Residence Accidentally Unearthed Seven Coffins Dating Back to the State's Early Settlement October 15, 2026 China Has an Ancient Tradition of Building Beautiful Paper Kites October 15, 2026 See the Stunning Winners of the Wildlife Photographer of the Year Contest, Capturing the Splendor and Drama of Nature October 14, 2026 A New Contender for the World's Oldest Shipwreck Has Been Discovered Off the Coast of Turkey.
