records.content: 24/7 LiveLos AngelesOrange CountyInland EmpireVentura CountyCalifornia 87° Bald Eagle Big Bear bald eagle Jackie's cause of death revealed in new necropsy report Big Bear's beloved bald eagle Jackie died from complications related to highly pathogenic avian influenza, according to necropsy results. KABC Thursday, October 15, 2026 3:58PM Share BIG BEAR, Calif. (KABC) -- Big Bear's beloved bald eagle Jackie died from complications related to a type of infectious avian flu, according to necropsy results. The California Department of Fish and Wildlife, San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance and Ojai Raptor Center on Wednesday released the results of testing conducted after Jackie's death, shedding new light on the illness that veterinarians had been trying to diagnose during weeks of treatment. The findings determined that highly pathogenic avian influenza, or bird flu, was the primary underlying cause of Jackie's decline. "Jackie's necropsy confirmed Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) as the primary underlying cause of her decline," said Steve Kubiski, director of disease investigations for the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance. "In an uncommon presentation of the virus, the infection caused a severe ulcer in her stomach that led to persistent internal bleeding, anemia, and the development of bacterial sepsis." The damage also allowed bacteria to enter her body, resulting in a serious secondary infection. Additional testing found evidence of the virus in multiple tissues. The results help explain the severe anemia that veterinarians were battling while caring for Jackie at the Ojai Raptor Center earlier this year. Jackie spent more than three weeks receiving intensive treatment, including oxygen therapy and a life-saving blood transfusion, as experts worked to determine what was making her sick. Toxicology testing detected brodifacoum, a rodent poison, in Jackie's liver. However, officials said the findings did not show the type of uncontrolled bleeding associated with the poison, and it was not identified as the primary cause of her illness or death. "The necropsy results have helped connect many of the findings we were seeing throughout the eagle's hospitalization," said Chris Eksteen, executive director of Ojai Raptor Center. "We are grateful to the many veterinary specialists, laboratories, wildlife agencies and partner organizations who worked alongside our team to understand her illness and provide her with the best possible care. Caring for her was an extraordinary privilege for our entire team." Big Bear's beloved bald eagle Jackie, who had been receiving intensive medical care for a prolonged illness, has died. See the timeline of her rescue and treatment here. Jackie died Aug. 10 after her condition continued to deteriorate despite treatment. Her remains were later cremated by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's National Eagle Repository, according to wildlife officials. "The story of the Big Bear bald eagle reflects the powerful connection people feel to these iconic birds," said CDFW Director Meghan Hertel. "We're grateful to everyone who cared for her and worked to support her well-being. Understanding the results of these tests is an important part of learning from this case and can help inform the care and treatment of other eagles and wildlife in the future." Jackie's death marked the loss of one half of the iconic bald eagle pair that had occupied Big Bear Valley for years. Her mate, Shadow, remains in the area, and officials said there is no evidence that he or the pair's eaglets became sick. Jackie gained a worldwide following through the Friends of Big Bear Valley eagle camera, with millions of viewers tuning in over the years to watch her and Shadow raise their young. Wildlife officials said her story helped bring attention to bald eagles, conservation and the habitats they depend on. He covers breaking news throughout Southern California. When he's not writing about local events, he enjoys focusing on sports and entertainment. Read Full Bio Dean Fioresi Updated on: October 14, 2026 / 9:56 PM PDT / CBS LA Add CBS News on Google Big Bear bald eagle Jackie's cause of death has been revealed nearly two months after she died in August, following weeks of testing and rehabilitation. According to the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, a necropsy and additional testing determined that Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza, or HPAI, was the "primary underlying cause of her decline." "In an uncommon presentation of the virus, the infection caused a severe ulcer in her stomach that led to persistent internal bleeding, anemia, and the development of bacterial sepsis," said Steve Kubiski, the Director of Disease Investigations with the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, which performed the necropsy. Jackie, who was estimated to be around 14 years old, died nearly a month after she was rescued from the Big Bear Lake shoreline, where she was found after being seen in a fight with two subadult eagles in July. Jackie, the Big Bear bald eagle who captured the awe of millions over the years via the Big Bear Bald Eagle Nest Cam. Friends of Big Bear Valley A team of veterinary experts at the Ojai Raptor Center oversaw her care in the weeks that followed, documenting the process as they tried to nurse her back to health. Despite undergoing a blood transfusion, which briefly provided a glimpse of hope, Jackie continued to suffer setbacks in her recovery due to the sickness, which remained a mystery until Wednesday's announcement by California wildlife officials. "Jackie showed signs of chronic disease involving the ventriculus, the muscular portion of a bird's stomach, commonly called the gizzard. The damaged and ulcerated tissue contributed to ongoing blood loss and her persistent severe anemia," the CDFW release said. "It also allowed bacteria to enter the body, resulting in a serious secondary bacterial infection." Officials said that additional testing also revealed severe inflammation and blood clot formation in Jackie's heart and several major blood vessels, and that the HPAI virus genetic material was present in several tissues throughout her body, including the ulcerated tissue in her ventriculus. Other tests showed Jackie was negative for West Nile Virus, and heavy metal levels were within acceptable limits. While toxicology screening detected brodifacoum, an anticoagulant rodenticide, in Jackie's liver, the necropsy did not find uncontrolled bleeding typically associated with the chemical pesticide, so it was not identified as her primary cause of illness or death. "Together, the findings showed that Jackie was suffering from multiple severe and interconnected disease processes that had been developing over time and ultimately led to her decline and death," CDFW's release said. Jackie and Shadow in 2024. Friends of Big Bear Valley Jackie's remains were cremated by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's National Eagle Repository, following the established procedures intended to prevent the transmission of HPAI to wildlife or humans, the release said. "The story of the Big Bear bald eagle reflects the powerful connection people feel to these iconic birds," said a statement from CDFW Director Meghan Hertel. "We're grateful to everyone who cared for her and worked to support her well-being. Understanding the results of these tests is an important part of learning from this case and can help inform the care and treatment of other eagles and wildlife in the future." Jackie was an iconic fixture in Southern California, drawing the attention of millions across the United States thanks to the 24/7 livestream camera documenting her life and that of her partner, Shadow, from above Big Bear Lake. Over the years, the duo parented several clutches of eaglets, most recently Sandy and Luna. CDFW officials said that based on camera data, they have no evidence to suggest that Shadow or the eaglets were sick. "Jackie's story brought unprecedented public attention to bald eagles and the importance of protecting the habitats they depend on," the release from CDFW said. "Her life and the public's connection to her highlights the powerful role that wildlife can play in connecting people to conservation." In the weeks since her death, Jackie has been honored with a massive memorial service in Big Bear, a life-size monument at a park in the San Bernardino Mountains and an Ontario Tower Buzzers minor league baseball game dedicated to celebrating her life. California state legislators also passed a resolution in her honor, proclaiming September 4 as California Wildlife Day. Facebook Linkedin Threads Whatsapp Reddit Email Page link A recent study has proposed a road map for countries to better monitor wildlife health and disease outbreaks. Previous research found that nearly 60% of the 107 countries it surveyed showed no evidence of a functional wildlife health surveillance system. This leaves ecosystems, agriculture, and human populations vulnerable to catastrophic outbreaks, the researchers say. The blueprint presented in the latest study offers actionable solutions to improve surveillance, said study co-author Sarah Olson, director of health at the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS). “Earlier research did a good job diagnosing the problem in terms of what’s missing, and what wildlife health surveillance needs to deliver,” Olson told Mongabay by email. “This paper goes further: it uses a Theory of Change to map out how we actually close that gap, given limited resources and fragmented networks, to reach real collaborative surveillance. The challenge now is scaling efforts and expertise through a global community of practice — no single organization can meet this need alone, and the more we collaborate, the faster surveillance can grow everywhere.” Olson and her colleagues write that unmonitored disease events have already inflicted severe ecological and economic damage; for instance, sheep and goat plague caused an estimated 80% decline in Mongolia’s endangered saiga antelope (Saiga tatarica), while highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1) continues to trigger mass mortality across populations of wild birds and marine mammals. Mongabay recently reported on the spread of H5N1 affecting wild birds, urban wildlife, and live animal markets across cities like New York. The researchers say that if lethal pathogens can spread unchecked in heavily monitored megacities, the risks are vastly magnified in regions lacking basic biosurveillance. However, existing monitoring efforts remain plagued by sporadic, crisis-driven funding that evaporates as soon as emergencies subside, according to the researchers. To overcome these systemic barriers, the study outlines a collaborative road map or “theory of change” designed by the Wildlife Health Intelligence Network (WHIN) to establish lasting, locally led surveillance programs. The road map identifies six pathways. This includes shifting mindsets away from viewing wildlife merely as an economic liability; securing dedicated political support and funding; and adopting evidence-based practices. A fourth pathway includes deploying user-driven tools like the shared HAWK data platform, a service for managing wildlife health surveillance data. The other steps include strengthening frontline workforce skills, and mobilizing a global community of practice. Rather than imposing top-down mandates, the road map advocates scaling up proven regional models, such as WildHealthNet in Southeast Asia, to integrate community monitoring directly into national legislation. The authors noted that many of the recognized experts in this field are in high-income countries, creating a significant limitation in global representation. But Olson said the network is intentionally structured to reverse that imbalance, “by elevating local expertise from low- and middle-income countries along with Indigenous-led and community-led efforts.” Banner image: Dead elephant seal pups on a beach in Argentine Patagonia. It’s unclear how they died. Image © Maxi Jonas via WCS. Please reference surfaced articles to validate AI summary Explore DeeperDive Full Summary Jackie, the famed bald eagle from Big Bear Lake, died in August from complications of highly pathogenic avian influenza that caused a severe stomach ulcer, internal bleeding, anemia and bacterial sepsis, as detailed in a necropsy report released in October 2026. Jackie, the beloved California bald eagle whose life was watched via live video feeds by millions around the world, died of complications resulting from avian influenza, according to a newly released necropsy report. "Jackie's necropsy confirmed Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) as the primary underlying cause of her decline," Steve Kubiski, director of disease investigations for the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, said in a statement Wednesday, Oct. 14. "In an uncommon presentation of the virus, the infection caused a severe ulcer in her stomach that led to persistent internal bleeding, anemia, and the development of bacterial sepsis." The newly released report sheds light on the mysterious illness that veterinarians struggled to treat throughout the summer. The Big Bear Lake, California, bald eagle's life was livestreamed on YouTube, leading to her becoming an object of global fascination and to her hometown becoming practically synonymous with America's iconic bird. She died in August after a weeks-long fight with an illness that confounded the eagle's doctors. Efforts to save Jackie saw her hospitalized and placed under anesthesia for veterinarians to perform what many hoped would be a life-saving blood transfusion. Veterinary pathologists at the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance performed the necropsy. According to the report released by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, the avian flu left Jackie with a severe stomach ulcer that led to ongoing blood loss and ultimately a deadly bacterial infection. "Together, the findings showed that Jackie was suffering from multiple severe and interconnected disease processes that had been developing over time and ultimately led to her decline and death," the California Department of Fish and Wildlife said of the report. The state agency said that HPAI is a highly infectious disease that has been circulating in wild bird populations throughout the United States. Eagles and other raptors are believed to contract the disease through contact with infected birds or by eating infected prey. Waterfowl and shorebirds are natural carriers of the viruses. Jackie was hatched in 2012, the first eaglet to do so in Big Bear Valley, USA TODAY previously reported. Her parents, Ricky and Lucy, became the first known adult eagles who decided to stay in Big Bear Valley, which until then had only been a part-time winter destination for the species. Big Bear Lake is about an hour northeast of San Bernardino in Southern California. She lived in Big Bear Valley in the San Bernardino National Forest. She became a viral sensation a few years later when U.S. Forest Service employee Sandy Steers got the idea to install a webcam 120 feet off the forest floor to broadcast her life. Jackie found her first romance in 2017 when she mated with an eagle named Mr. B. The couple's eggs hatched in 2018, and while one of the eaglets died after a 24-hour rainstorm, the other, named Stormy, survived and left Big Bear that summer. Her second mate, Shadow, remains in Big Bear, state authorities said. California wildlife officials said that there is nothing to indicate he or their eaglets, Sandy and Luna, are sick. "The story of the Big Bear bald eagle reflects the powerful connection people feel to these iconic birds," said wildlife agency Director Meghan Hertel. "We’re grateful to everyone who cared for her and worked to support her well-being. Understanding the results of these tests is an important part of learning from this case and can help inform the care and treatment of other eagles and wildlife in the future." records.content: Yona Tugg and colleagues show that a polyclonal secretory immunoglobulin A preparation, purified from breast milk pooled from multiple donors, neutralized respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), human adenovirus type 5, and H1N1 and H3N2 influenza A viruses in laboratory assays. In mouse models of H1N1 influenza infection, two intranasal doses of LCTG-001, given two hours before and 24 hours after infection, reduced illness and lung damage in both immunocompetent and antibody-deficient mice. In immunocompetent mice, lung viral loads were lower early in infection but comparable to controls later, despite less lung damage and better lung barrier integrity. The findings support further study of mucosal passive immunization for individuals with antibody deficiencies, although efficacy in humans has not been established. LCTG-001 could also be a candidate for seasonal influenza prevention and pandemic response, the researchers suggest. Tugg et al. produced the purified IgA product from breast milk collected from 120 donors through milk banks in Indianapolis and Pittsburgh. LCTG-001 also bound proteins and virus-like particles from H5N1 avian influenza viruses in clade 2.3.4.4b, but showed little neutralizing activity against the H5N1 strain tested; protection against H5N1 was not tested in animals. In laboratory assays, LCTG-001 inhibited influenza neuraminidase activity and stimulated human neutrophils when complexed with influenza antigens; the contribution of these activities to protection in mice remains unresolved. Source: Journal reference: Tugg, Y., et al. (2026). Polyclonal breast milk–derived secretory IgA confers broad antiviral protection against multiple respiratory viruses. Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aef3207. https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aef3207

records.content: News Health Breast milk antibodies reduced lung damage in mice — News-Medical UA.NEWS 15 October 2026 05:53 In the United States, the breast milk antibody preparation LCTG-001 reduced disease manifestations and lung damage in mice infected with the H1N1 influenza virus. The study used purified polyclonal secretory immunoglobulin A obtained from pooled breast milk from donors. Results of experiments in mice As News-Medical reports , the animals received two intranasal doses of the preparation: two hours before infection and 24 hours afterward. The effect was recorded both in mice with normal immune systems and in animals with antibody deficiency. In mice with normal immune systems, the amount of virus in the lungs was lower than in the control group at the early stage of infection. Later, the viral load became comparable to that in the control group; however, animals that received the preparation had less lung damage and better lung barrier function. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram . Activity against several viruses In laboratory tests, LCTG-001 neutralized respiratory syncytial virus, human adenovirus type 5, and influenza A viruses of the H1N1 and H3N2 subtypes. The preparation also inhibited influenza virus neuraminidase activity and stimulated human neutrophils when it formed complexes with influenza antigens. At the same time, researchers have not yet established the role of these mechanisms in protecting mice. Breast milk from 120 donors, collected through milk banks in Indianapolis and Pittsburgh in the United States, was used to produce LCTG-001. The preparation bound to proteins and virus-like particles of H5N1 avian influenza clade 2.3.4.4b, but showed little neutralizing activity against the tested H5N1 strain. Its protective effect against this virus was not tested in animals. The researchers note that the results justify further study of passive mucosal immunization for people with antibody deficiencies. The effectiveness of LCTG-001 in humans has not yet been established. Read us on Download our app

时间:2026年10月14日 来源:Poultry Science 4.5 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 Open access 家禽养殖场良好的生物安全实践可改善动物健康、福利和生产性能,但不同养殖场间的实施差异很大。反复发生的高致病性禽流感(HPAI)暴发以及具有户外通道的更高福利系统的扩张,引发了对暴露风险可能存在差异的担忧。然而,生物安全实施在不同生产系统间的差异程度仍不清楚。研究人员开展了一项横断面比较研究,以评估荷兰肉鸡养殖场中与HPAI相关的生物安全实践和风险因素,比较集约化系统(仅室内)和粗放化系统(生长较慢的肉鸡并具有带顶棚户外通道)。该研究纳入78个养殖场(63个集约化和15个粗放化)。生物安全使用Biocheck.UGent调查的统一化子集进行评估。从40个可比变量中,根据与HPAI引入和传播途径的相关性选择28个变量。采用带马蹄形先验(horseshoe priors)的贝叶斯逻辑回归(Bayesian logistic regression)评估生产系统间差异。大多数生物安全措施在系统间没有显著差异,在集约化和粗放化养殖场内均观察到相当大的变异。估计差异最大的是尸体储存清洁、饲养密度和雏鸡运送频率,尽管这些差异的统计学支持程度不一。饲养密度和运送频率反映系统间的结构性差异,而尸体储存清洁反映管理实践差异。这些发现表明,针对养殖场特定薄弱环节、辅以量身定制生物安全计划和现场指导的干预措施,可能比仅基于系统的建议更有效。 kg/m2;粗放化使用慢速生长品种,周期56至81天,密度较低,常提供户外通道。这些结构差异可能以不同方式影响暴露途径。生物安全(biosecurity)是降低HPAI传入及农场内和农场间传播的主要手段,包括外部生物安全(防止病原进入)和内部生物安全(限制进入后传播)。关键传入途径包括污染车辆和设备、人员移动、直接或间接接触野鸟。但生物安全实施和依从性在农场间差异很大。当前研究主要关注常规系统,对生产系统与生物安全要求和HPAI风险关联的评估有限,且“集约化”和“粗放化”定义不一致限制跨研究比较。使用统一化、与HPAI相关措施直接比较集约化和粗放化肉鸡系统的研究很少。荷兰同时存在常规仅室内肉鸡生产和慢速生长肉鸡加户外通道的替代概念,因此可在同一国家法规背景下比较。研究人员假设,虽然系统水平结构特征不同,但各系统内农场间生物安全实践仍存在显著变异。 关键技术方法:研究人员开展横断面比较研究(cross-sectional comparative study),纳入78个荷兰肉鸡养殖场。63个集约化农场来自Biocheck.UGent数据库(2015至2023年调查),15个粗放化农场于2023年12月至2024年5月通过专业网络招募并现场访问。使用Biocheck.UGent调查的统一化子集,将两版问卷协调后保留40个可比变量,并依据与HPAI传入和传播途径的相关性选择28个变量。主要统计方法为带正则化马蹄形先验(regularized horseshoe prior)的贝叶斯逻辑回归(Bayesian logistic regression),以生产系统为二分类结局;同时进行描述统计、最小-最大归一化热图、时间、先验和模型敏感性分析,以及Pareto平滑重要性抽样留一法交叉验证(Pareto-smoothed importance-sampling leave-one-out, PSIS-LOO)和近似受试者工作特征曲线下面积(area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, AUC)。 研究结果: 在78个养殖场中比较生物安全(63个集约化,15个粗放化)。通过横断面调查与统一化Biocheck.UGent变量比较,未显示系统间清楚分离。 集约化与粗放化养殖场未分离成不同组,且未出现一致的系统水平模式。热图显示,集约化农场36个分类变量均有多于1个反应类别,粗放化农场34/36如此;粗放化农场仅有饲养密度和清空禽舍步骤数无变异。若干变量在两系统均呈持续高风险:饲料筒仓清洁与消毒、饲料运送频率、访客无禽期要求、与静水或流水邻近。其中水邻近和饲料运送频率反映固定环境或结构特征,其余与农场管理实践相关。 在28个变量中,绝对后验均值系数最大的3个分类变量为尸体储存清洁、饲养密度和雏鸡运送频率。贝叶斯模型以集约化=0、粗放化=1编码生产系统,系数描述控制其他变量后各反应类别与生产系统的关联,不是因果效应;负系数表示与集约化农场关联,正系数表示与粗放化农场关联。尸体储存清洁方面,以“总是”清洁为参考,“有时”清洁后验均值系数为–2.38(95%可信区间[credible interval, CrI] –6.28至0.06;负系数后验概率0.93),提示该反应更常见于集约化农场,但95% CrI包括零;“从不”和“无独立尸体储存”接近零且区间宽。描述结果显示,61.9%(39/63)集约化农场报告“有时”清洁,粗放化农场为0/15;60.0%(9/15)粗放化农场报告“总是”清洁。饲养密度以“不超过33 kg/m2”为参考,超过33 kg/m2的后验均值系数为–3.22(95% CrI –7.05至0.02;负系数后验概率0.96),提示高密度在粗放化农场较少见,但95% CrI包括零;所有粗放化农场(15/15)密度不超过33 kg/m2,71.4%(45/63)集约化农场超过该阈值。雏鸡运送频率以“少于3次”为参考,“3至6次”后验均值系数为+1.08(95% CrI –0.22至4.59;正系数后验概率0.80),提示粗放化农场更常处于中等频率,但方向支持较弱且95% CrI包括零;“超过6次”接近零。描述结果显示,93.3%(14/15)粗放化农场每年3至6次,65.1%(41/63)集约化农场超过6次。其余23个分类变量和雇佣人数后验均值接近零但可信区间宽,不能解释为系统间相似;经理经验每年系数较小(后验均值–0.05,95% CrI –0.14至0.01;负系数后验概率0.94)。近似PSIS-LOO交叉验证AUC为0.94,反映该数据集内农场分离而非可推广预测性能。 时间敏感性分析显示集约化农场总体模式大致稳定,但若干变量在时期之间有描述性变化,尤其饲养密度、分多步清空禽舍、装卸区清洁消毒和经理经验。超过33 讨论部分总结与结论翻译: 讨论指出,本研究旨在识别荷兰肉鸡农场生物安全实施变异,并评估其是否系统性与生产系统相关。通过统一化Biocheck.UGent子集比较28个HPAI相关措施,发现有限证据支持生产系统间系统性差异,两组内均有显著变异。最大估计差异涉及尸体储存清洁消毒、饲养密度和雏鸡运送频率,但统计支持不一。近零系数不能因整体变异小解释;观察到的变异似乎分布在个体农场而非与生产系统一致,但仅15个粗放化农场且变量多,估计不精确,宽可信区间不能排除中等系统差异。若干措施在两系统均持续高风险,提示行业共同薄弱环节,包括饲料筒仓清洁、访客无禽期等,改善实施不太可能仅依赖意识。尸体储存清洁是唯一直接可修改管理实践且敏感性分析最一致;但尸体储存配置理解可能影响回答,荷兰家禽产业链质量方案(IKB Kip)允许尸体储存整合于禽舍而非物理独立设施。饲养密度是明确结构差异,绝大多数集约化超过33 kg/m2,粗放化无一超过,符合欧盟定义;不应视为生物安全差或HPAI传入风险高,且不等于农场或群体规模。2003年荷兰H 7 N 7 疫情中较大农场规模与HPAI传入相关,而饲养类型无关;近期模型显示较小农场规模降低模拟HPAI流行规模,但未完全抵消户外农场增加带来的传入风险和流行规模增加。雏鸡运送频率对比更弱,反映生产周期长度;欧洲食品安全局(EFSA)评估欧盟内活禽包括一日龄雏鸡移动导致HPAI传入可能性为不太可能。频繁雏鸡运送本身不应解释为更高HPAI传入风险,还取决于接触周围生物安全措施;集约化农场更常报告雏鸡运输车辆装车前清洁消毒(61/63对8/15),但该变量未纳入模型。实践意义是生产系统单独为生物安全实施的有限代理,干预应针对农场特定薄弱环节;Biocheck.UGent可用于基准评估和识别改进领域,兽医指导可改善家禽农场生物安全评分。政策应补充系统级法规与农场级实施支持,行业组织在雏鸡运送物流、饲料运输和尸体收集等需协调措施中有作用。同时,一般生物安全措施相似实施不代表系统间HPAI暴露相同,户外通道可能增加直接或间接接触野鸟和污染环境的机会,这种系统特定暴露未被统一化措施捕获。局限包括观察与自报混合、非随机抽样、集约化样本来自便利样本且可能偏向更高生物安全意识、粗放化农场数少、时间差异、横断面设计、残余混杂、排除系统特定问题以及风险评分未与HPAI发病率关联。 研究结论翻译:总之,大多数与HPAI相关的生物安全措施在集约化和粗放化肉鸡农场之间呈现重叠的反应分布,每个系统内农场间存在显著变异。在最大对比中,尸体储存清洁是唯一直接可修改的实践,并且在敏感性分析中最一致,而饲养密度和雏鸡运送频率主要反映系统的结构性特征。这些发现表明,仅生产系统不能充分反映实践中的生物安全表现。因此,生物安全改进应同时针对农场特定薄弱环节和整个行业共同的实施缺口。同时,一般生物安全措施的相似实施并不能消除系统特定暴露途径,特别是与户外通道相关的暴露途径。未来研究应在更大规模和纵向研究中验证这些发现,纳入系统特定暴露途径(如户外系统中野生鸟类接触),评估农场定制生物安全干预和现场指导是否能带来可测量的实施与疾病预防改善,并确定此处发现的共同薄弱环节是否也存在于其他国家和生产系统。 –0.14至0.01;负系数后验概率0.94)。近似PSIS-LOO交叉验证AUC为0.94,反映该数据集内农场分离而非可推广预测性能。时间敏感性分析显示集约化农场总体模式大致稳定,但若干变量在时期之间有描述性变化,尤其饲养密度、分多步清空禽舍、装卸区清洁消毒和经理经验。超过33 kg/m比例从2022年前78.7%(37/47)降至之后50.0%(8/16)。由于所有粗放化农场均在2022年后调查,模型无法完全分离时间和系统差异;将调查时期作为协变量后,超过33 kg/m系数从–3.22减弱至–1.31,而尸体储存清洁关联仍一致(调整前后–2.38和–2.82)。先验和模型敏感性分析对该3个变量估计大致相似;排除结构性系统关联变量后尸体储存清洁关联仍一致。讨论部分总结与结论翻译:讨论指出,本研究旨在识别荷兰肉鸡农场生物安全实施变异,并评估其是否系统性与生产系统相关。通过统一化Biocheck.UGent子集比较28个HPAI相关措施,发现有限证据支持生产系统间系统性差异,两组内均有显著变异。最大估计差异涉及尸体储存清洁消毒、饲养密度和雏鸡运送频率,但统计支持不一。近零系数不能因整体变异小解释;观察到的变异似乎分布在个体农场而非与生产系统一致,但仅15个粗放化农场且变量多,估计不精确,宽可信区间不能排除中等系统差异。若干措施在两系统均持续高风险,提示行业共同薄弱环节,包括饲料筒仓清洁、访客无禽期等,改善实施不太可能仅依赖意识。尸体储存清洁是唯一直接可修改管理实践且敏感性分析最一致;但尸体储存配置理解可能影响回答,荷兰家禽产业链质量方案(IKB Kip)允许尸体储存整合于禽舍而非物理独立设施。饲养密度是明确结构差异,绝大多数集约化超过33 kg/m,粗放化无一超过,符合欧盟定义;不应视为生物安全差或HPAI传入风险高,且不等于农场或群体规模。2003年荷兰H疫情中较大农场规模与HPAI传入相关,而饲养类型无关;近期模型显示较小农场规模降低模拟HPAI流行规模,但未完全抵消户外农场增加带来的传入风险和流行规模增加。雏鸡运送频率对比更弱,反映生产周期长度;欧洲食品安全局(EFSA)评估欧盟内活禽包括一日龄雏鸡移动导致HPAI传入可能性为不太可能。频繁雏鸡运送本身不应解释为更高HPAI传入风险,还取决于接触周围生物安全措施;集约化农场更常报告雏鸡运输车辆装车前清洁消毒(61/63对8/15),但该变量未纳入模型。实践意义是生产系统单独为生物安全实施的有限代理,干预应针对农场特定薄弱环节;Biocheck.UGent可用于基准评估和识别改进领域,兽医指导可改善家禽农场生物安全评分。政策应补充系统级法规与农场级实施支持,行业组织在雏鸡运送物流、饲料运输和尸体收集等需协调措施中有作用。同时,一般生物安全措施相似实施不代表系统间HPAI暴露相同,户外通道可能增加直接或间接接触野鸟和污染环境的机会,这种系统特定暴露未被统一化措施捕获。局限包括观察与自报混合、非随机抽样、集约化样本来自便利样本且可能偏向更高生物安全意识、粗放化农场数少、时间差异、横断面设计、残余混杂、排除系统特定问题以及风险评分未与HPAI发病率关联。研究结论翻译:总之,大多数与HPAI相关的生物安全措施在集约化和粗放化肉鸡农场之间呈现重叠的反应分布,每个系统内农场间存在显著变异。在最大对比中,尸体储存清洁是唯一直接可修改的实践,并且在敏感性分析中最一致,而饲养密度和雏鸡运送频率主要反映系统的结构性特征。这些发现表明,仅生产系统不能充分反映实践中的生物安全表现。因此,生物安全改进应同时针对农场特定薄弱环节和整个行业共同的实施缺口。同时,一般生物安全措施的相似实施并不能消除系统特定暴露途径,特别是与户外通道相关的暴露途径。未来研究应在更大规模和纵向研究中验证这些发现,纳入系统特定暴露途径(如户外系统中野生鸟类接触),评估农场定制生物安全干预和现场指导是否能带来可测量的实施与疾病预防改善,并确定此处发现的共同薄弱环节是否也存在于其他国家和生产系统。
